examTip.mnemonic: **Principal planes: no shear. Maximum-shear planes: at 45° to them, carrying a normal stress of (σ₁+σ₂)/2.** On Mohr's circle the principal points are where it crosses the σ axis and the maximum-shear points are the top and bottom — 90° apart on the circle, hence 45° in reality.

questions.stem: A floating body attains stable equilibrium if its metacentre is:
questions.solution:
**Above the centroid** (that is, above the centre of gravity G).

When a floating body tilts slightly, the submerged shape changes and the **centre of buoyancy B** shifts sideways. The **metacentre M** is where the new line of action of the buoyant force crosses the original centreline. Stability then depends entirely on whether M lies above or below G:

| Position of M | GM | Couple produced | Equilibrium |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Above G** | **Positive** | **Righting** — restores the body | **Stable** |
| Coincident with G | Zero | None | Neutral |
| Below G | Negative | Overturning | **Unstable** |

With **M above G**, the upward buoyant force through the shifted B and the downward weight through G form a couple that pushes the body **back** to upright. If M falls below G the same couple acts in the tilting direction and the body capsizes.

**Computing the metacentric height:**

> **GM = BM − BG = I/V − BG**

where I is the second moment of area of the **water-plane section** about the axis of tilt and V the displaced volume. So a **wide** hull has a large I and is stiff; a narrow one is tender. Experimentally,

> GM = (w·x)/(W·tan θ)

by shifting a known weight w a distance x across the deck and measuring the tilt θ.

**The design tension**, which the examination likes: a **large** GM gives strong stability but a short, violent rolling period,

> T = 2π√(k²/(g·GM))

uncomfortable and hard on the structure. A **small** positive GM gives an easy roll but little margin. GM is therefore chosen as a compromise rather than maximised.

Note the contrast with a **fully submerged** body — a submarine or a balloon — where the displaced shape does not change on tilting, so the metacentre concept does not apply at all. There stability requires simply that **B lie above G**.

The same fact is examined from the formula side in Set 3 Q37 and Set 2 Q86.

examTip.trap: Applying the **submerged**-body rule (B above G) to a **floating** body is the standard error. Almost every ship floats with **B below G** and is perfectly stable.
examTip.trick: For a floating body **B MOVES** as it heels, because the displaced volume changes shape. That is what creates the metacentre.
examTip.mnemonic: **GM = BM − BG, with BM = I/V and I ∝ beam³** — which is why a wide raft is stable and a log rolls. **Submerged bodies are the different case**: B is fixed, BM = 0, so B really must be above G — hence a submarine's ballast in the keel.

questions.stem: The neutral stress in a soil mass is:
options: Stress taken up by the pore water
Stress taken up by solid particles
questions.solution:
**The stress taken up by the pore water** — the **pore water pressure**, u.

Terzaghi's principle of effective stress divides the total stress at a point between the water and the soil skeleton:

> **σ = σ′ + u**

| Component | Name | Carried by |
|---|---|---|
| σ | Total stress | Everything |
| **u** | **Neutral stress / pore water pressure** | **The pore water** |
| σ′ | **Effective stress** | The **soil skeleton** — grain to grain |

**Why "neutral".** Water cannot sustain shear, and it presses **equally in all directions** on every surface of a particle. It therefore does not push grains against one another and contributes nothing to shear strength — it is neutral with respect to the soil's mechanical behaviour. Under hydrostatic conditions it is simply

> u = γ_w · h_w

the depth below the water table times the unit weight of water.

**Everything mechanical depends on σ′, not σ**, and that is the single most important idea in soil mechanics:

> **Shear strength:** τ = c′ + σ′ tan φ′
> **Consolidation:** settlement occurs as u dissipates and σ′ rises
> **Bearing capacity, earth pressure, slope stability:** all computed on effective stress

So raising the water table raises u, lowers σ′, and **reduces strength** without any change in the total load — which is exactly why:

| Situation | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **Monsoon slope failure** | u rises, σ′ falls, τ falls; the factor of safety roughly **halves** under steady seepage (Set 2 Q45) |
| **Quick sand / boiling** | Upward seepage drives σ′ **to zero**; the soil has no strength at all (Set 1 Q3, Set 2 Q85) |
| **Liquefaction** in an earthquake | Cyclic shaking generates excess u in loose saturated sand; σ′ collapses |
| **Consolidation settlement** | Slow transfer of load from water to skeleton as u dissipates |

The distractors (a) and (b) are not defined quantities — there is no "neutral area" or "effective area" in the theory; the division is of **stress**, not of area. Option (d) describes **effective** stress, the complement of the right answer.

examTip.trick: **Neutral stress** is another name for **pore water pressure u**. It is called neutral because water carries no shear — it contributes nothing to strength.
examTip.mnemonic: **σ = σ′ + u: total = effective + neutral.** The whole of soil mechanics is that one line. Only σ′ governs strength, stiffness and volume change — which is why raising the water table weakens soil without changing the total stress at all.

questions.stem: The aggregate containing moisture in its pores and having its surface dry is known as:
questions.solution:
**Saturated surface dry (SSD) aggregate.**

SSD is the condition in which the aggregate's **pores are full of water** but there is **no free water on the surface**. That is precisely the state described — moisture inside, surface dry — and it is the standard reference condition for concrete mix design.

The four moisture states, in order of increasing water content:

| State | Pores | Surface | Effect on the mix |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Very dry (oven dry)** | **Empty** | Dry | **Absorbs** mix water; stiffens the concrete |
| Air dry / dry | **Partly** filled | Dry | Absorbs some mix water |
| **Saturated surface dry** | **Full** | **Dry** | **Neutral — the design reference** |
| Moist (wet) | Full | **Free water** | **Adds** water; raises w/c and lowers strength |

**Why SSD is the reference.** In this state the aggregate neither takes water from the mix nor gives water to it, so the water–cement ratio actually achieved is the one that was designed. Every other state introduces an error that must be corrected for.

**The correction in practice**, which is where this matters on site. Aggregate is almost never at SSD when it arrives:
- If **wetter** than SSD, the **free surface moisture** is subtracted from the batch water.
- If **drier** than SSD, water equal to the **absorption deficit** is added.

Omitting that correction is a common cause of a mix failing to reach its design strength, since even a small unaccounted increase in water raises the w/c ratio appreciably.

**A note on the printed options.** The source's own four-way classification defines its "dry aggregate" as one that "may contain some moisture in the pores but has a dry surface", which overlaps the wording of the stem. The distinction intended is one of degree: in **SSD the pores are completely full**, whereas in the source's "dry" category they are only partly filled. Since the stem names no partial filling and SSD is the established technical term for pores-full-surface-dry, (d) is the intended and correct answer — but a candidate could reasonably be delayed by the overlap.

Related: **water absorption** (the SSD-to-oven-dry difference) should be under about 2% for good aggregate, and **bulking** of damp sand — up to 20–40% volume increase — is a separate effect requiring its own correction in volume batching (Set 1 Q55, Set 2 Q27).

verification.notes: The source's own classification calls a partly-filled, dry-surfaced aggregate 'dry aggregate', which overlaps the stem's wording. SSD is the established term for pores fully saturated with a dry surface and is the keyed and intended answer; the overlap is noted in the solution.

examTip.trick: **SSD** means pores **full** but surface **dry** — the aggregate neither absorbs mix water nor adds free water. It is the neutral reference condition for mix design.
examTip.mnemonic: **SSD is the zero point.** Drier than SSD, the aggregate **steals** mix water and the concrete stiffens; wetter, it **contributes** water, the w/c ratio rises and strength falls. On site, aggregate moisture must be measured and the batch water corrected **every time** — this is one of the commonest sources of variable concrete.

questions.stem: A projecting piece usually provided to support a truss is:
questions.solution:
**Option (c) is the keyed answer, but the question is defective: the correct term is "corbel", which is not offered.**

**What the source itself says.** The answer sheet keys (c), frieze — and then, in the same explanation, defines: *"Corbel: it is a projecting stone that is usually provided to serve as support for roof truss, beam, weather shed, etc."* That is a verbatim description of the stem, and it names **corbel**, which does not appear among the four options.

The source's own definitions of the terms that *are* offered:

| Term | What it actually is |
|---|---|
| **Corbel** | **A projecting stone supporting a roof truss, beam or weather shed** ← what the stem describes |
| **Frieze** | A course of stone immediately **below the cornice**, along the external face — decorative, supports nothing |
| **Cornice** | A projecting **ornamental** course near the top of a wall, or at a wall–ceiling junction |
| **Coping** | A course on the **exposed top** of an external wall, to shed water and prevent seepage |
| **Lintel** | A beam **across an opening**, carrying the masonry above it |
| String course | A horizontal projecting course, to throw rainwater off the face |

So none of the four options is correct. A **frieze** is a decorative band, not a bracket; a **cornice** projects but is ornamental; a **coping** caps a wall; a **lintel** spans an opening rather than projecting from a wall.

**What to carry forward.** The useful distinction is between the projecting members and what each does: a **corbel** carries a concentrated load (truss, beam), a **cornice** and **string course** throw water clear of the face, a **coping** protects the wall top, and a **lintel** spans an opening. The word "projecting" alone does not settle it — the question is what the projection *carries*.

The keyed answer is retained so the paper matches the original sitting, but this item is flagged: it has no correct option, and the owner should replace it or add "corbel" as a choice.

verification.notes: The question has no correct option. The source's own explanation identifies the described member as a CORBEL, which is absent from the four choices; a frieze is a decorative course below the cornice and supports nothing. The keyed letter (c) is retained to match the original paper, but the item should be replaced or amended to include 'corbel' before use in a paid set.

examTip.trick: Sort the entablature and support terms by position: the **corbel or bracket** projects to support a load; the **frieze** is a decorative horizontal band; the **cornice** is the projecting crown moulding.
examTip.mnemonic: **A corbel/bracket CARRIES; a frieze and cornice DECORATE.** A corbel is designed as a short deep cantilever — and because its span/depth is small it fails in **shear-friction**, not flexure, which is why its detailing rules are special.

questions.stem: For testing a saturated clay for shear strength, the test recommended is:
questions.solution:
**Unconfined compression test.**

The unconfined compression test is the special case of a triaxial test with the **cell pressure set to zero**, σ₃ = 0. A cylindrical specimen is loaded axially until it fails, and

> **c_u = q_u / 2**

where q_u is the unconfined compressive strength. It gives the **undrained shear strength** directly, with **φ_u = 0**, which is exactly the parameter wanted for a saturated clay under rapid loading.

**Why it suits saturated clay specifically:**
- Saturated clay has such low permeability that loading is effectively **undrained**, so the φ = 0 analysis is the appropriate one.
- The test is **quick, simple and cheap**, needing no cell, no pressure supply and no drainage measurement.
- It is the basis of the standard consistency classification, and of the field **pocket penetrometer**.

Consistency by unconfined compressive strength:

| q_u (kPa) | Consistency |
|---|---|
| < 25 | Very soft |
| 25 – 50 | Soft |
| 50 – 100 | Medium |
| 100 – 200 | Stiff |
| 200 – 400 | Very stiff |
| > 400 | Hard |

**Why not the others.** The **direct shear (box shear) test** is unsuitable for clay: drainage cannot be controlled, pore pressure cannot be measured, and the failure plane is **forced** to be horizontal rather than forming on the soil's own weakest plane. That alone disposes of option (d), "all the above".

The **triaxial test** is not wrong — it is in fact the more complete test, and where **effective-stress** parameters c′ and φ′ are needed it is the only option, because drainage and pore pressure can both be controlled (Set 3 Q85). But for the routine determination of a saturated clay's undrained strength, the unconfined compression test is the recommended and standard method.

A caution: the test **cannot be used on fissured or sandy clay**, since without lateral confinement such a specimen fails prematurely along a fissure and under-reports the strength. For those soils the triaxial test is necessary. The **vane shear** test (Set 2 Q64) serves the same purpose *in situ*, and additionally yields the **sensitivity** by re-testing the remoulded soil.

examTip.trick: The unconfined compression test applies **no cell pressure**, so it is only valid where the specimen can stand on its own and where **φ_u = 0** — that is, saturated clay tested undrained.
examTip.mnemonic: **q_u = 2c_u — the Mohr circle's radius is c_u and its diameter is q_u.** The test is quick and needs no cell, but it **cannot be used on sand or fissured clay**, and for anything important the **triaxial** test is preferred because it controls drainage and measures pore pressure.

questions.stem: In which of the following conditions can the Bernoulli equation not be used?
questions.solution:
**Viscous flow.**

Bernoulli's equation is derived by integrating Euler's equation along a streamline, and Euler's equation assumes an **ideal (inviscid) fluid** — one with **zero viscosity**. Where viscosity is present, energy is dissipated as friction, so the total head is **not** conserved and the equation in its basic form fails.

The assumptions behind
> p/γ + v²/2g + z = constant

are:

| Assumption | Note |
|---|---|
| **Inviscid (non-viscous)** | **The one violated in option (a)** |
| **Steady** flow | Option (c) — a *required* condition, not a violation |
| **Incompressible** | Option (b) — likewise required |
| Along a **streamline** | The constant belongs to that streamline |
| Irrotational | Needed for the constant to be the same for *all* streamlines |
| Gravity and pressure the only body forces | No external work or heat |

So options (b) and (c) are conditions under which Bernoulli **does** apply — they are prerequisites, not obstacles. That is the trap the question sets.

**Option (d), laminar flow**, deserves a note. Laminar flow is by nature viscosity-dominated, so it too falls outside the strict Bernoulli assumptions — but "viscous" names the offending property directly and generally, while "laminar" names a flow regime. Since a **turbulent** flow is also viscous and also non-conservative, (a) is the correct and complete answer.

**How real flows are handled.** The equation is extended with a loss term rather than abandoned:

> p₁/γ + v₁²/2g + z₁ = p₂/γ + v₂²/2g + z₂ + **h_L**

where h_L collects the major loss (Darcy–Weisbach, h_f = fLV²/2gD) and the minor losses (k·V²/2g at bends, valves, entries and exits). Add **+ h_pump** or **− h_turbine** where machinery does or extracts work, and essentially all pipeline analysis follows.

The graphical form of the same statement — the **EGL always falling in the direction of flow, and lying above the HGL by the velocity head** — is the subject of Set 3 Q16, and it is the falling EGL that is the visible signature of viscosity.

examTip.trick: Bernoulli assumes **frictionless** flow. Where viscosity matters, energy is lost and the constant is no longer constant — a **head loss term** must be added.
examTip.mnemonic: **Bernoulli fails wherever losses are large or unknown: viscous flow, sudden expansions, hydraulic jumps.** The rule to carry: **use ENERGY where losses are small or known; use MOMENTUM where they are large or unknown but the FORCES are what you need** — momentum does not require the losses to be quantified.

questions.stem: A shaft is subjected to bending moment M and a torque T simultaneously. The ratio of the maximum bending stress to the maximum shear stress developed in the shaft is:
questions.solution:
**2M/T.**

**Step 1 — maximum bending stress**, from the flexure formula M/I = σ/y with I = πd⁴/64 and y = d/2:

> σ = M(d/2)/(πd⁴/64) = **32M/(πd³)**

**Step 2 — maximum shear stress**, from the torsion formula T/J = τ/r with J = πd⁴/32 and r = d/2:

> τ = T(d/2)/(πd⁴/32) = **16T/(πd³)**

**Step 3 — the ratio.** The πd³ cancels completely:

> σ/τ = (32M/πd³) ÷ (16T/πd³) = 32M/16T = **2M/T** ✓

The factor of 2 comes from the ratio of the two section constants, **J = 2I** for a circular section — the only place the geometry enters, and the reason the answer is independent of the diameter.

The pair worth memorising, since they differ only in that factor:

| Loading | Maximum stress in a solid circular shaft |
|---|---|
| **Bending** | σ = **32M/πd³** |
| **Torsion** | τ = **16T/πd³** |

**Where this leads in design.** A shaft carrying M and T together is designed on **equivalent** actions, which combine the two into a single check:

> **Equivalent bending moment:** M_e = ½[M + √(M² + T²)]
> **Equivalent torque:** T_e = √(M² + T²)

The first is used with the maximum principal stress theory and the second with the maximum shear stress theory; the shaft diameter is taken as the larger of the two requirements. Both reduce to the simple cases when one action is absent.

For a **hollow** shaft the same logic applies with J = π(D⁴ − d⁴)/32 and I = π(D⁴ − d⁴)/64, so the ratio σ/τ is still exactly 2M/T — hollow sections being far more efficient, since removing the lightly stressed core saves weight while barely reducing either section constant.

examTip.trick: **Equivalent bending moment M_e = ½[M + √(M² + T²)]** and **equivalent torque T_e = √(M² + T²)**. Form the ratio the question asks for and simplify.
examTip.mnemonic: **T_e = √(M² + T²) always; M_e is half of (M + T_e).** These are the **maximum principal stress** and **maximum shear stress** theories applied to a shaft — which is why the two give different equivalent values.

questions.stem: The minimum cube strength of concrete used for a pre-stressed member is:
questions.solution:
**350 kg/cm²**, that is **M35**.

The conversion is the arithmetic the question turns on:
> 1 N/mm² = 10 kg/cm²
> so **35 N/mm² = 350 kg/cm²** ✓

IS 1343 requires a minimum grade of **M40 for post-tensioned** and **M30 for pre-tensioned** work in current practice; the figure of M35 quoted here is the traditional general minimum, and it is the value the options are built around.

**Why prestressed concrete demands such high strength**, which is the substance of the question:

| Reason | Explanation |
|---|---|
| **High local stresses at transfer** | The full prestress is delivered into a small anchorage or transfer zone; low-grade concrete would crush |
| **Lower creep and shrinkage** | Both are **losses of prestress**. Dense, high-strength concrete creeps and shrinks less, so more of the prestress survives |
| **Higher modulus of elasticity** | Reduces the elastic shortening loss |
| **Better durability** | The tendons are highly susceptible to corrosion; a dense, impermeable cover is essential |
| **Early strength gain** | Transfer can occur sooner, speeding production of precast units |

The second and third rows are the important ones: the time-dependent losses — creep, shrinkage and relaxation — consume **15 to 20%** of the initial prestress (Set 2 Q91), and low-grade concrete would consume considerably more, leaving an unreliable margin.

**The corresponding steel** is also high-strength: high-tensile wire or strand of about **1500 to 1900 N/mm²**, against 500 N/mm² for ordinary Fe 500 reinforcement. Prestressing is fundamentally a technique of **high-strength materials at both ends** — ordinary mild steel would relax too much and ordinary concrete would creep too much for the prestress to be worth applying.

The advantage bought by all this: the section is **pre-compressed**, so applied load must first overcome that compression before any tension — and hence any cracking — appears. The result is a crack-free member under service load, longer spans for the same depth, lighter sections, and no loss of stiffness from cracking.

examTip.trick: Prestressed concrete needs **high-strength concrete** for three reasons at once: it must resist the large **transfer** stresses at the anchorage, it must have **low creep and shrinkage** (which cause prestress loss), and it must have a **high modulus** to limit elastic shortening.
examTip.mnemonic: **Minimum M35 for post-tensioned and M40 for pre-tensioned work in IS 1343.** Prestressing steel is also very high strength (1500–1900 N/mm²) — necessary because the **losses of 15–25%** would consume most of the prestress in ordinary mild steel.

questions.stem: Zeolite used in the zeolite softening process for the treatment of hard water gets exhausted after a certain time of usage but can be regenerated by flushing it with:
questions.solution:
**10% sodium chloride solution** — brine.

**How zeolite softening works.** Sodium zeolite (a base-exchange medium, natural or synthetic resin) exchanges its **sodium** ions for the **calcium and magnesium** ions that constitute hardness:

> Ca(HCO₃)₂ + Na₂Ze → CaZe + 2NaHCO₃
> MgSO₄ + Na₂Ze → MgZe + Na₂SO₄

The hardness ions are captured on the bed and harmless sodium ions pass into the water.

**Why it exhausts, and how regeneration reverses it.** Once all the sodium sites have been taken by calcium and magnesium, the bed can capture no more and is exhausted. Flushing with a **concentrated (10%) brine** drives the exchange backwards by mass action — the sheer excess of Na⁺ displaces the Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺:

> CaZe + 2NaCl → Na₂Ze + CaCl₂
> MgZe + 2NaCl → Na₂Ze + MgCl₂

The bed is restored to the sodium form, and the calcium and magnesium chlorides are washed to waste.

The reason the other options fail is immediate: the regenerant must supply **sodium**, since sodium is what the bed has lost. Calcium or magnesium salts would supply exactly the ions being removed.

**Characteristics of the process:**

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Hardness removed | **Both temporary and permanent — down to almost zero** |
| Regenerant | **10% NaCl (brine)** |
| Requirement | Water must be **low in turbidity** (< 10 NTU) and free of iron and manganese, or the bed clogs |
| Limitation | **Adds sodium** to the water; removes no other impurity |

Compare with the **lime–soda process**, the alternative: it removes both hardnesses too but leaves a residual of 40 to 60 mg/L, produces large volumes of sludge, and needs skilled control — whereas zeolite is compact, automatic and achieves near-zero hardness, at the cost of sodium addition and a brine supply.

Since zeolite removes hardness completely, the softened water is usually **blended** with raw water to leave a modest residual hardness, because water of zero hardness is corrosive to pipes and flat in taste. This links back to Q19 of this paper: boiling removes only the **temporary** (bicarbonate) hardness, whereas zeolite removes both.

examTip.trick: Zeolite (base exchange) softening swaps **calcium and magnesium for sodium**. To regenerate, the resin is flooded with a **strong sodium chloride brine**, which drives the exchange backwards.
examTip.mnemonic: **Regenerate with brine — mass action reverses the exchange.** The trade-off: zeolite softening gives **near-zero hardness but raises the SODIUM content**, which matters for people on salt-restricted diets and for boiler feed. Lime-soda softening leaves residual hardness but does not add sodium.

questions.stem: According to Bligh's creep theory, percolating water flows along:
options: Straight path under the foundation of the dam
Circular path under the foundation of the dam
The outline of the base of the foundation of the dam
questions.solution:
**The outline of the base of the foundation.**

Bligh's **creep theory** (1910) makes the simplest possible assumption about seepage beneath a hydraulic structure: the water "creeps" along the **contact surface between the structure's base profile and the subsoil**, following every horizontal run and every vertical cut-off in turn. The total length of that path is the **creep length**:

> **L = b + 2d₁ + 2d₂ + 2d₃ + …**

where b is the horizontal floor length and d₁, d₂, d₃ the depths of the cut-offs. Each cut-off contributes **twice** its depth, because the water travels down one face and up the other.

Bligh further assumed the head is lost **uniformly** along that path, so the hydraulic gradient is constant:

> H/L = 1/C
where C is **Bligh's coefficient of creep** — 12 for coarse gravel, 15 for coarse sand, up to 18 for fine micaceous sand. The safety requirement is that the creep length provided must be at least **C × H**, and its reciprocal L/H is the creep coefficient.

**The theory's two fatal assumptions**, which is why it has been superseded:

| Bligh assumed | Reality (Khosla) |
|---|---|
| Head lost **uniformly** along the creep path | Head loss is **non-uniform**, following potential flow |
| Horizontal and vertical creep **equally effective** | **Vertical cut-offs are far more effective** than horizontal floor length |

Bligh therefore over-values horizontal creep and under-values vertical creep — and, more seriously, gives no way of computing the **exit gradient**, which is the quantity that actually governs **piping** failure at the downstream end.

**Khosla's theory** replaced it, using potential flow theory with correction factors, and it does deliver the exit gradient:

> G_E = (H/d) · 1/(π√λ)

which is compared against the critical hydraulic gradient (≈ 1) with a factor of safety of 4 to 5. **Lane's weighted creep theory** sits between the two, weighting vertical creep three times as heavily as horizontal.

Set 5 Q56 examines the same theory from the other side — asking what Bligh assumed about the relative weighting of horizontal and vertical creep, the answer being that he treated them as equal.

examTip.trick: Bligh's **creep length** is measured along the **contact surface between the structure's base and the soil** — the shortest path a water particle can travel beneath the work.
examTip.mnemonic: **Bligh weighted vertical and horizontal creep EQUALLY, and that is his theory's fatal flaw** — vertical cut-offs are far more effective per metre. **Lane** weighted vertical 3:1; **KHOSLA** abandoned creep entirely and solved the actual flow, showing that safety depends on the **EXIT GRADIENT** and the **downstream cut-off**.

questions.stem: Which one of the following linings is suitable for shield driven tunnels, particularly in subaqueous regions?
questions.solution:
**Cast iron lining.**

A subaqueous tunnel — driven beneath a river or seabed — faces two demands that only a metal segmental lining can meet:

| Demand | Why cast iron answers it |
|---|---|
| **Watertightness** | Bolted segments with machined faces and caulked joints form a **sealed** ring; masonry cannot |
| **High external hydrostatic pressure** | Cast iron is strong in **compression**, and a circular ring carries external pressure as pure hoop compression |
| Immediate support behind the shield | Segments are **erected and bolted at once**, inside the shield tail |
| Resistance to corrosion in wet ground | Cast iron corrodes far more slowly than steel |

That combination is why cast iron segmental linings were the standard for river and underwater tunnels, and why the other options fail:

- **Brick and stone linings** are jointed masonry: **not watertight**, and they cannot resist high external water pressure without leaking.
- **Timber** rots in a permanently wet environment; it serves only as **temporary** support during driving.

**Where it fits in the method.** In **shield tunnelling**, a cylindrical shield is jacked forward while excavation proceeds at the face under its protection. The lining ring is erected within the tail of the shield, and the shield's forward jacks thrust against the completed rings. In soft, water-bearing ground the face may additionally be supported by **compressed air**, slurry or an earth-pressure balance machine.

Modern practice has largely replaced cast iron with **bolted precast concrete segments** carrying elastomeric gaskets — cheaper, and watertight when the gaskets are properly compressed — with **ductile iron** or fabricated steel segments retained for the highest pressures and for special cross-passages. The engineering requirement, however, is unchanged: a **sealed, compression-carrying ring**.

The tunnel lining options in general: no lining (sound rock), **shotcrete** with rock bolts and mesh (the NATM approach), cast in-situ concrete, precast segments, and steel or cast iron segments — chosen by ground condition, water pressure and the driving method.

examTip.trick: **Cast iron segmental lining** is bolted up **inside the shield** as it advances, giving immediate ring support in soft, water-bearing ground where nothing else would stand.
examTip.mnemonic: **Shield tunnelling in soft ground needs a lining erected WITHIN the shield tail** — segmental cast iron or precast concrete. In **rock**, where the ground stands unsupported for a time, shotcrete and rock bolts (**NATM**) are used instead. The ground condition, not the diameter, chooses the method.

questions.stem: The minimum thickness of the base of a flexible pavement is:
questions.solution:
**10 cm (100 mm).**

The base course of a flexible pavement is normally provided in the range **100 to 300 mm**, so 100 mm is the minimum.

**Why a minimum exists at all.** The base is the principal load-spreading layer: it receives the concentrated wheel load from the surfacing and distributes it over a wide enough area for the sub-base and subgrade to carry. Below about 100 mm a granular layer cannot:

- develop the **interlock** needed to act as a coherent layer — it behaves as loose material;
- be **compacted** properly, since a layer thinner than roughly twice the maximum aggregate size cannot be rolled effectively;
- spread the load through a meaningful depth.

The layers of a flexible pavement and their usual thicknesses:

| Layer | Thickness | Function |
|---|---|---|
| **Surface (wearing) course** | **25 – 50 mm** | Resists wear and weather; waterproofs; gives riding quality |
| Binder course | 50 – 100 mm | Transfers load from surface to base |
| **Base course** | **100 – 300 mm** | **Main load-spreading layer** |
| Sub-base | 100 – 300 mm | Further spreading; drainage; separation from subgrade |
| Compacted subgrade | 150 – 300 mm | Prepared natural ground |

The bituminous coats between them are examined alongside: a **prime coat** on the granular base to seal and bond it, a **tack coat** between successive bituminous layers, and a **seal coat** on the surface.

**How the thicknesses are actually determined.** They are not chosen from this table but designed, from two inputs (IRC 37 / DoR guidelines):

> **Subgrade CBR** — the strength of the foundation (Set 3 Q97)
> **Cumulative standard axles (CSA)** — the design traffic, computed with the vehicle damage factor and the **lane distribution factor** (Set 3 Q68)

A weak subgrade or heavy traffic demands a thicker total pavement. The table's ranges are the practical bounds within which that design falls.

The governing principle, from Set 1 Q99: a flexible pavement transmits load by **grain-to-grain contact**, the stressed area widening with depth. Hence the layers are arranged in **decreasing order of strength downward**, and the thickness required is fixed by what the subgrade can bear.

examTip.trick: The minimum thickness of a granular base is a **practical** limit — thinner layers cannot be compacted properly, because the aggregate is comparable in size to the layer.
examTip.mnemonic: **The compacted layer must be at least 2–3 times the maximum aggregate size**, or the roller simply pushes the stones around. That is the general rule behind every minimum layer thickness in pavement construction.

questions.stem: A milestone chart:
options: Shows the interdependencies of various jobs
Depicts the delay of jobs, if any
Points outgoing ahead of schedule of jobs, if any
questions.solution:
**None of these.**

A milestone chart is an **improvement on the bar (Gantt) chart**, but only a modest one. It divides each long bar at identifiable key events — **milestones** — so that progress *within* an activity becomes visible instead of being hidden until the bar ends.

What it can and cannot do:

| Capability | Milestone chart |
|---|---|
| Shows activities against a time scale | **Yes** |
| Shows key events in **chronological** order | **Yes** |
| Gives better **control** than a plain bar chart | **Yes** |
| Shows **interdependencies** between jobs | **No** |
| Shows the **logical** sequence | **No** |
| Identifies the **critical path** | **No** |
| Handles **time uncertainty** | **No** |

So option (a) is explicitly wrong: interdependency is the very thing a milestone chart **cannot** represent, and that limitation is why network techniques were developed. Options (b) and (c) describe what a **progress review against the plan** tells you, not a property of the chart form itself — a milestone chart records where the milestones fell, but it cannot say what a delay will *do* to the project, because it does not know what follows what.

**The evolution of planning techniques**, which puts the milestone chart in its place:

| Order | Technique | Advance | Limitation |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Bar (Gantt) chart**, c. 1917 | Activities on a time scale | No logic; progress within a bar invisible |
| 2 | **Milestone chart**, 1940s | Bars broken at key events | **Still no interdependency or logic** |
| 3 | **CPM**, 1957 | **Network logic**; identifies the critical path; deterministic durations | No treatment of uncertainty |
| 4 | **PERT**, 1958 | Network with **probabilistic** durations | Considers only the critical path's variance |

The decisive step is the third: only a **network** can answer the question a manager actually needs answered — *which* delay matters. A delay on the critical path (zero total float) delays the whole project; a delay elsewhere may be absorbed by float. A milestone chart cannot distinguish the two, which is exactly its shortcoming and the reason the answer here is "none of these".

In modern practice the two are combined: planning software computes network logic internally while **displaying** it as a bar chart, because a bar chart remains the most readable form for communication.

examTip.trick: A milestone chart marks **key dates or events** on a bar chart — it shows *when* things should happen but **not the dependencies** between activities.
examTip.mnemonic: **Bar chart → milestone chart → network (CPM/PERT).** Each step adds information: the bar chart shows duration, the milestone chart flags key events, and only the **network shows DEPENDENCY and hence the CRITICAL PATH**. That last is what neither of the first two can do.

questions.stem: The technique for establishing and maintaining priorities among the various jobs of a project is known as:
questions.solution:
**Critical ratio scheduling.**

Critical ratio scheduling ranks jobs by how urgent each is relative to how long it will take, using a single index:

> **Critical ratio = Demand time / Supply lead time**

where the demand time is the time remaining until the job is needed and the supply lead time is the time still required to complete it.

Interpreting the index — this is the whole technique:

| CR | Meaning | Action |
|---|---|---|
| **< 1.0** | **Behind schedule** — less time remains than the work needs | **Expedite; highest priority** |
| **= 1.0** | Exactly on schedule | Monitor |
| **> 1.0** | **Ahead of schedule**, has slack | Can be deferred |

So jobs are sequenced in **increasing order of critical ratio**: the most negative margin is worked on first. Because the ratio is recomputed as work proceeds, priorities **update dynamically** — a job that was comfortable becomes urgent as its demand time shrinks, without anyone having to re-plan the whole programme. That self-updating property is what makes it a technique for *maintaining* priorities and not merely establishing them once.

The alternatives named in the options:

| Technique | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Critical ratio scheduling** | **Establishes and maintains priorities** among jobs by the CR index |
| Event flow scheduling | Based on the **work breakdown structure**; events and activities interconnected in logical sequence |
| Short interval scheduling | Selects **one** operation among several to execute from a ready state — very short horizon |
| Slotting technique | Divides operations into **time slots** so they do not conflict during execution |

**Where it is used.** Critical ratio scheduling comes from **job-shop and production** scheduling, where many jobs compete for the same machines, and it transfers naturally to construction whenever limited resources — a crane, a batching plant, a specialist crew — must be allocated among competing activities.

Note how it differs from the **critical path**: the critical path identifies which activities cannot be delayed *at all* without delaying the project, while the critical ratio ranks *all* jobs by relative urgency at a given moment. The two are complementary — CPM sets the plan, the critical ratio helps decide what to do first when the plan comes under pressure.

examTip.trick: **Critical ratio = (time remaining) ÷ (work remaining)**. A ratio below 1 means the job is behind and needs priority; above 1 means it has slack.
examTip.mnemonic: **Critical ratio below 1 = behind schedule = act now.** It is a **dynamic** priority rule — the ratio is recalculated as work proceeds, so priorities shift automatically, unlike a fixed sequence.

questions.stem: For the movement of vehicles at an intersection of two roads, without any interference, the type of grade separator generally preferred is:
questions.solution:
**Clover leaf.**

The phrase to seize on is **"without any interference"**. That means **complete separation of traffic** — no vehicle crossing another's path, and no left or right turns conflicting with through movements. Only a full clover leaf achieves that at a four-way crossing of two major highways.

A **clover leaf** has **four legs and eight ramps**: in each quadrant one direct ramp and one indirect (loop) ramp. Every turning movement is made by merging and diverging, never by crossing, so all conflict points are eliminated.

The interchange types and where each is used:

| Type | Legs | Character |
|---|---|---|
| **Clover leaf** | **4** | **Full separation, no crossing conflicts**; needs a large area |
| **Diamond** | 4 | Simple, compact, cheap — but the ramp terminals **cross the minor road at grade**, so conflicts remain |
| **Trumpet** | **3** | Standard solution for a **T junction** |
| **Delta** | 3 | Another three-leg form, with a triangular island |
| Directional | 4 | Direct high-speed ramps for major movements; expensive, used on freeways |
| Rotary interchange | 4 | Roundabout at one level, through road at the other |

So the **diamond** is the near miss: it is a grade separator, but its ramps meet the crossroad at grade and therefore *do* involve interference — which is precisely what the question excludes. And the **trumpet** and **delta** are three-leg forms, unsuitable for an intersection of two roads.

**The cost of a clover leaf** is worth knowing alongside its merit: it requires a very **large land area**, the loop ramps have small radii and so impose **low speeds**, and it creates **weaving sections** where vehicles entering and leaving must cross one another between successive ramps. Weaving capacity, rather than ramp capacity, often governs its performance — which is why partial clover leaves and directional interchanges are used where land or capacity demands it.

The general hierarchy of intersection treatment, from least to most expensive: **at-grade uncontrolled → channelised → signalised → rotary → grade-separated interchange**. Grade separation is justified only by high volumes, high speeds or a poor accident record, since the cost step is large.

examTip.trick: A **clover leaf** is a grade-separated interchange in which every turning movement is made by a **ramp**, so no two traffic streams cross at grade — traffic **weaves** and merges but never conflicts head-on.
examTip.mnemonic: **Grade separation removes CROSSING conflicts; a roundabout converts them to WEAVING; a signal separates them in TIME.** Three different answers to the same problem, at three very different costs. A clover leaf needs a lot of land, which is why diamond interchanges are commoner in constrained sites.

questions.stem: In a reaction turbine, when steam flows through the fixed blades:
questions.solution:
**Pressure decreases while velocity increases.**

The **fixed blades** (nozzles or guide vanes) act as a **nozzle**: the passage between them converges, so the fluid accelerates. By the energy equation, that acceleration must be paid for out of pressure energy — so as velocity rises, pressure falls.

> Pressure energy → kinetic energy

That is the defining function of the fixed row: to direct the flow onto the moving blades *and* to accelerate it.

**What distinguishes a reaction turbine** is what happens next. In the **moving** blades the pressure falls *again*, so expansion is shared between both rows:

| | Fixed blades | Moving blades |
|---|---|---|
| **Impulse turbine** | Pressure **drops**, velocity rises | Pressure **constant**; velocity falls as work is done |
| **Reaction turbine** | Pressure **drops**, velocity rises | Pressure **drops again**; the blades act as nozzles too |

So in a reaction machine the pressure falls **continuously** through the stage, which is why the runner must be enclosed and fully flooded, and why the **degree of reaction** — the fraction of the total enthalpy or head drop occurring in the moving blades — is a design parameter (50% in a Parsons turbine).

**The hydraulic parallel**, which is what this syllabus is really about. In a water turbine the same distinction holds:

| | **Impulse (Pelton)** | **Reaction (Francis, Kaplan)** |
|---|---|---|
| Where pressure is converted | **Entirely in the nozzle**, before the runner | **Partly in the guide vanes, partly across the runner** |
| Runner operates at | **Atmospheric** pressure | **Above** atmospheric; fully submerged |
| Casing | Not pressurised | Pressurised scroll case |
| **Draft tube** | **Not required** | **Required** — recovers residual kinetic energy |
| Cavitation risk | Negligible | **At runner exit**, the lowest-pressure point |

The last two rows follow directly from the pressure distribution: because a reaction turbine still has pressure to give up at runner exit, it needs a draft tube to recover it — and because that point is the pressure minimum, it is where **cavitation** occurs (Set 3 Q95).

So the answer to this question and the need for a draft tube are two consequences of the same fact: **in a reaction machine, expansion continues through the runner.**

examTip.trick: In a **reaction** turbine the pressure **drops across the runner** while the relative velocity increases — that pressure drop is what distinguishes it from an impulse machine.
examTip.mnemonic: **Reaction: pressure changes across the runner, which therefore runs FULL and needs a DRAFT TUBE. Impulse (Pelton): all the head becomes velocity in the nozzle, and the runner works at atmospheric pressure in air.** That single difference explains every other difference between the two families.

questions.stem: Guide banks are provided to:
options: Train the flow of a river along a specified course
questions.solution:
**To train the flow of a river along a specified course.**

Guide banks (Bell's bunds) are earthen embankments built on either side of a bridge or barrage. Their function is to **guide the river axially** through the structure's waterway, gathering the flow in from a wide, meandering flood plain and delivering it square to the opening — and, in doing so, protecting the approach embankments from being outflanked.

Why the other options are wrong, and the distinctions matter:

| Option | Why it fails |
|---|---|
| **Reduce peak flood discharge** (b) | Guide banks do **nothing** to the discharge — that would require **storage** (a reservoir or detention basin). Training works redirect flow; they do not reduce it |
| **Confine the width of river** (c) | A **consequence**, not the purpose. Confinement is how the guiding is achieved, and over-confinement causes **afflux** and deeper scour |
| **Increase the waterway** (d) | The opposite of what happens — the waterway is **narrowed** to a designed width |

Option (c) is the closest and deserves the care: confining the width is a means, whereas **guiding the flow axially** is the end. A river approaching a bridge obliquely attacks one abutment and scours it, however wide the opening.

**Design proportions**, examined repeatedly:

| Feature | Value |
|---|---|
| **Upstream length** | **1.0 L to 1.5 L** (L = waterway length) |
| **Downstream length** | **0.2 L to 0.4 L** |
| Bell mouth (curved head) radius | ≈ 0.45 L; sweep 120° to 145° upstream, 45° to 90° downstream |
| Side slopes | 2H : 1V, **stone pitched** |
| Toe protection | **Launching apron** — gabions or loose stone (Set 2 Q34) |

The upstream arm is much the longer because that is where the work is done: the flow must be gathered and turned over a long distance. Downstream it need only be released and allowed to expand (Set 1 Q79, Set 2 Q76).

**The waterway itself** is fixed by **Lacey's regime perimeter, P = 4.75√Q**, using the **dominant discharge** — capped by the actual bank-to-bank width where that is narrower (Set 2 Q74). The anticipated scour depth, from R = 0.47(Q/f)^{1/3}, then fixes how far the launching apron must extend and how deep the foundations go.

The other river training works, for contrast: **spurs / groynes** (deflect flow away from a bank), **revetments and pitching** (armour the bank in place), **cut-offs** (shorten a meander), and **levees** (confine flood water to the channel).

examTip.trick: Guide banks (Bell's bunds) **confine a braided or meandering river** to the bridge or barrage waterway and stop it **outflanking** the structure by cutting a new course round the abutment.
examTip.mnemonic: **Upstream arm 1.0–1.25 L, downstream 0.2–0.4 L** — much longer upstream, because that arm must intercept and steer the approaching flow, which takes distance. They are protected by **launching aprons**, which are designed to be undermined and to fall into the scour hole.

questions.stem: A manhole is classified as shallow if its depth is between:
questions.solution:
**0.7 to 0.9 m.**

Manholes are classified by depth, because the depth determines the size, the construction and whether a person must enter:

| Class | Depth | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Shallow** | **0.7 – 0.9 m** | At the **head of a branch sewer**, or where traffic is light. Also called an **inspection chamber** |
| **Medium / normal** | 0.9 – 1.5 m | 1000 × 1000 mm or 800 × 1000 mm in plan |
| **Deep** | **> 1.5 m** | Requires **steps or ladder**; heavy cover; larger chamber |

**What manholes are for.** They give access to the sewer for **inspection, cleaning and rodding**, and they are the points at which the sewer's **ventilation** occurs. Because a sewer must be capable of being cleared along its whole length, manholes are required at every point where rodding could not otherwise reach:

- Every **change of direction, gradient, diameter or alignment**
- Every **junction** of two or more sewers
- At **regular intervals** on straight runs — about 30 m for sewers up to 0.3 m diameter, rising to 90 m or more for large sewers
- At the **head** of every branch

**Special types** examined alongside:

| Type | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **Drop manhole** | Where an incoming sewer is much higher than the outgoing one — the drop is taken inside the chamber to avoid scour |
| **Flushing manhole** | At the head of a branch on a flat gradient, to flush out deposits |
| **Junction chamber** | Where large sewers meet |
| Lamphole | Small opening for inspection only, no entry |

Construction details: brick or RCC chamber, **benching** of the floor sloped towards the channel so solids are not left standing, a **cast iron or RCC cover** (heavy duty where under traffic), and step irons in deep manholes.

Two safety points that matter in practice. A manhole is a **confined space** containing **hydrogen sulphide** — toxic, and it deadens the sense of smell so it gives no warning — and **methane**, which is explosive. Entry requires ventilation, gas testing and a standby person at the surface. And the air space above the sewage, which the manhole ventilates, is exactly where H₂S is oxidised by bacteria into **sulphuric acid**, causing the **crown corrosion** that destroys concrete sewers from the inside top (Set 3 Q40).

examTip.trick: Manhole depth classes determine the size and the access arrangement: **shallow** (no step irons needed), **normal**, and **deep** (step irons or a ladder required).
examTip.mnemonic: **Manholes are placed at every change of direction, gradient, size or level, at junctions, and at straight-run intervals** (about 30 m for small sewers, more for large). They exist for **inspection, cleaning and ventilation** — the last being what protects the sewer crown from H₂S corrosion.

questions.stem: A fillet weld whose axis is parallel to the direction of applied load is known as:
questions.solution:
**Side fillet weld.**

Fillet welds are classified by the **orientation of the weld axis relative to the load**, and the terminology follows directly:

| Weld | Axis relative to load | Loaded in |
|---|---|---|
| **Side (longitudinal) fillet** | **Parallel** to the load | **Shear** along the throat |
| **End (transverse) fillet** | **Perpendicular** to the load | Combined shear and tension |
| Diagonal fillet | At an angle | Combined |

A **side fillet** transfers force by shearing along its length — the load runs parallel to the weld, so the throat is sheared longitudinally. An **end fillet** is crossed by the load and is therefore somewhat **stronger** for the same size, though IS 800 conservatively designs both on the same shear strength of the throat.

**The design strength**, common to both:

> Design strength per unit length = **t_e · f_u / (√3 γ_mw)**

with the effective throat **t_e = 0.7 s** for fusion faces at 60° to 90° (Set 2 Q92), f_u the smaller ultimate tensile strength of the parts joined, and γ_mw = **1.25 for shop** welding, **1.5 for site** welding — site welds derated because quality is harder to control.

**Rules that apply particularly to side fillets:**
- **Effective length** = actual length − 2s, allowing for the incomplete throat at each end; minimum **4s**.
- **End returns** of twice the weld size at each end, to protect against tearing.
- Where a side fillet is very long relative to its size, stress is **not uniform** along it — it concentrates at the ends — so IS 800 requires the strength to be reduced for lengths exceeding about 150 times the throat thickness.
- In an **unsymmetrical member** such as an angle connected by one leg, the side fillets must be proportioned so their **resultant passes through the centroid** of the member, or the connection is eccentric and develops a moment.

That last point is the practical trap: welding an angle with equal welds top and bottom looks tidy but loads it eccentrically. The welds are instead sized in inverse proportion to their distance from the centroid.

Contrast with a full-penetration **butt weld**, whose effective throat is the **full plate thickness**, so it develops the strength of the member itself — which is why butt welds are used for main tension members and fillet welds for connections and brackets.

examTip.trap: **Side (longitudinal)** and **end (transverse)** fillet welds are easy to reverse. The axis being **parallel** to the load makes it a side fillet.
examTip.trick: Picture the load path: a **side** fillet is sheared along its length; an **end** fillet is loaded across it.
examTip.mnemonic: **End fillets are about 30–40% STRONGER than side fillets** for the same size, because the stress distribution across the throat is more uniform. But both are designed on the **throat = 0.7 × size**, never on the leg length.

questions.stem: If the width of a simply supported beam carrying an isolated load at its centre is doubled, the deflection of the beam at the centre is changed by:
questions.solution:
**1/2** — the deflection is **halved**.

**Step 1 — the deflection formula:**
> δ = WL³/(48EI)

Everything except I is unchanged, so **δ ∝ 1/I**.

**Step 2 — how I responds to doubling the width.** For a rectangular section,
> I = bd³/12

The width b appears to the **first power**, so doubling b doubles I:
> I₂ = (2b)d³/12 = **2I**

**Step 3 — the new deflection:**
> δ₂ = WL³/(48E · 2I) = **δ₁/2** ✓

**The contrast that makes this question worth asking.** Compare doubling the **depth** instead:

| Change | Effect on I | Effect on δ |
|---|---|---|
| **Width b doubled** | I × **2** | δ **halved** |
| **Depth d doubled** | I × **8** (since d is cubed) | δ reduced to **1/8** |

So depth is **four times as effective as width** for the same amount of extra material. Option (b), 1/8, is precisely the answer to the depth version of the question — placed here to catch anyone who reaches for the d³ term without checking which dimension changed.

**That single fact explains most structural shapes.** It is why:
- a beam is turned **on edge** rather than laid flat;
- an **I-section** concentrates material in flanges as far from the neutral axis as possible, leaving only a thin web;
- a **deep, narrow** section is preferred wherever lateral stability allows.

The same d³ dependence governs strength as well as stiffness, through the section modulus Z = bd²/6 — though note that there the depth exponent is **2**, not 3, so depth is three times as effective as width for strength but four times for stiffness.

**The practical limit** on going ever deeper is **lateral-torsional buckling**: a very deep, thin beam will buckle sideways out of its plane before reaching its bending capacity, which is why deep beams need compression-flange restraint, and why IS 800 reduces the design bending strength for laterally unrestrained members.

examTip.trick: For a rectangular section **I = bd³/12**, so **I ∝ b** to the first power. Deflection **δ ∝ 1/I**, so doubling the width **halves** the deflection.
examTip.mnemonic: **Width is linear; DEPTH is cubed.** Doubling the width halves the deflection, but doubling the **depth** reduces it to **one eighth**. That is why beams are made deep and narrow, and why increasing depth is always the more effective remedy for a deflection problem.

questions.stem: The frictional resistance of a pipe varies approximately with …… of the liquid.
questions.solution:
**The square of the velocity.**

From the Darcy–Weisbach equation:

> **h_f = f L V² / (2 g D)**

so the friction head loss is proportional to **V²** — provided the friction factor f is treated as approximately constant, which it is in **turbulent** flow, the normal condition in engineering pipelines.

**The qualification "approximately" is doing real work here**, and the two regimes must be distinguished:

| Regime | Friction factor | Head loss varies as |
|---|---|---|
| **Laminar** (Re < 2000) | **f = 64/Re** — strongly dependent on V | **h_f ∝ V** (first power) |
| **Turbulent** (Re > 4000) | f nearly constant; f ≈ 0.316/Re^{0.25} for smooth pipes | **h_f ∝ V²** (approximately, hence "approximately") |

In laminar flow, f ∝ 1/V cancels one power of V², so the loss becomes **linear** in velocity — which is exactly what the Hagen–Poiseuille result gives:

> h_f = 32 μ V L / (γ D²)

In turbulent flow f varies only weakly with Re, so V² dominates and the square law holds. Since most water and sewage mains run turbulent, the V² relation is the practical rule — and it is what the question is after.

**Why this matters in design.** The V² dependence is severe. Doubling the velocity in a pipe **quadruples** the friction loss, and the pumping energy needed to overcome it. That is precisely why:

- **penstock and pipeline velocities are optimised** rather than maximised — the economic diameter balances the capital cost of a bigger pipe against the lifetime value of head lost to friction (Q21 of this paper);
- a modest increase in diameter pays for itself: since V ∝ 1/D² for a given Q, h_f ∝ 1/D⁵, so a small enlargement cuts the loss dramatically;
- **minor losses** are written in the same form, h_L = k V²/2g, so they too scale with V².

The **Moody diagram** ties it all together, plotting f against Re for a family of relative roughness values: a single line in the laminar zone (where roughness is irrelevant, because the viscous sublayer covers the wall), then a transition, then curves flattening to constant f in the **fully rough turbulent** zone — where the square law is exact rather than approximate.

examTip.trick: Read it off Darcy–Weisbach: **h_f = fLV²/(2gD)** — the V² is explicit. In fully rough turbulent flow f is constant, so the resistance goes as **V²** exactly.
examTip.mnemonic: **Laminar h_f ∝ V; fully rough turbulent h_f ∝ V².** Plotting **log h_f against log V** and reading the slope identifies the flow regime — that is the classic Reynolds pipe-friction experiment, and still how a laboratory rig is analysed.

questions.stem: A wall constructed with stones to protect slopes of cuttings in natural ground from the action of weathering agents is called:
questions.solution:
**Breast wall.**

The distinction between a breast wall and a retaining wall is one of **what the wall is holding**, and it is the whole point of the question:

| | **Breast wall** | **Retaining wall** |
|---|---|---|
| Built against | **Natural, undisturbed ground** — the face of a cutting | **Made-up ground / backfill** |
| Purpose | **Protects the face from weathering**, erosion and surface fall | **Resists active earth pressure** from the fill |
| Earth pressure | Small — the ground is self-supporting | **Full active pressure**, P_a = ½K_aγH² |
| Size | Smaller, lighter | Larger, designed for overturning and sliding |

A cut face in natural ground generally stands on its own, at least initially. What destroys it is **weathering**: rain washing out fines, freeze–thaw, wetting and drying, root action and small surface falls. A breast wall clads and protects that face. It is not designed to hold back a mass of soil, because the soil is not pushing.

Why the other options are wrong:
- A **buttress** is a pier projecting from a wall to give it **lateral support** and reduce its slenderness (Set 2 Q72).
- A **parapet wall** is a low wall at the **edge of a roof, terrace or bridge**, for safety.

**Why this matters in Nepal specifically.** Hill road construction produces thousands of kilometres of cut slopes, and their long-term stability is the dominant maintenance problem. Breast walls are among the standard protection measures, alongside **stone pitching, gabion walls, catch drains and bio-engineering** (vegetative slope protection, which the Department of Roads uses extensively).

The crucial companion measure is **drainage**. As Set 2 Q45 showed, steady seepage roughly **halves** the factor of safety of a slope, and Set 4 Q16 that wetting reduces the shear strength of cohesive soil. A breast wall built without weep holes and a cut-off drain behind it can therefore make matters **worse** — it traps water in the slope while adding its own weight. Every such wall needs **weep holes, a granular backing filter and a catch drain above the cut**.

That is the general lesson for hill slopes: **protection without drainage is not protection.**

examTip.trap: **Breast wall** and **retaining wall** are easily swapped. A **retaining** wall holds back **filled or made** ground; a **breast** wall supports **natural, undisturbed** ground in a cutting.
examTip.trick: Ask whether the soil behind was placed or was always there. Natural ground already stands at some angle, so a breast wall resists less pressure than a full retaining wall.
examTip.mnemonic: **Breast wall: natural slope in a cutting. Retaining wall: filled ground. Toe wall: at the base of an embankment.** All three appear constantly on Nepali hill roads, and **gabions** are the usual construction — flexible, permeable, and built from local boulders.

questions.stem: The radius of gyration of a rectangular section is not proportional to:
options: Square root of the moment of inertia
Square root of the inverse of the area
Square root of the moment of inertia divided by area of the section
questions.solution:
**None of these** — the radius of gyration is proportional to all three.

By definition:

> **k = √(I/A)**

Testing each option against that:

| Option | Claim | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| (a) √I | k ∝ √I, holding A constant | **True** |
| (b) √(1/A) | k ∝ 1/√A, holding I constant | **True** |
| (c) √(I/A) | k *equals* this | **True** |
| **(d) None of these** | k is proportional to all of them | **The answer** |

Since the question asks what k is **not** proportional to, and every option is something it *is* proportional to, the answer is (d).

Option (c) is the definition itself; (a) and (b) are the two halves of it read separately, each holding the other quantity fixed. There is no trick beyond reading the negative in the stem carefully.

**Values for a rectangle**, b × d:
> k_xx = √(I_xx/A) = √[(bd³/12)/(bd)] = **d/√12 = 0.289 d**
> k_yy = **b/√12 = 0.289 b**

so the radius of gyration about each axis is about **29%** of the dimension perpendicular to it — and the **minimum** k, which is the one that matters, is governed by the **smaller** dimension.

**Why k matters.** It is the quantity that converts a section's stiffness into a **slenderness ratio**:

> **λ = l_e / k_min**

and slenderness is what decides whether a compression member crushes or buckles:

> **σ_cr = π²E / λ²**

IS 800 caps λ at **180** for a member carrying dead and live load (250 for one resisting wind only). Because λ uses **k_min**, buckling always occurs about the **weak** axis — which is why a section is efficient as a column only when its two radii of gyration are comparable. That is precisely the reasoning behind the **ISSC** column section of Set 3 Q2, and why a deep narrow beam section makes a poor column.

Physically, k is the distance from the axis at which the entire area could be concentrated without changing I — a measure of how far the material is **spread** from the axis, which is exactly what resists buckling.

examTip.trick: **k = √(I/A)**, and for a rectangle about the centroidal axis **k = d/√12 ≈ 0.289d** — the **width cancels entirely**.
examTip.mnemonic: **The radius of gyration depends only on the dimension IN THE PLANE OF BENDING.** So widening a rectangular beam changes I and A in the same proportion and leaves k untouched — which is why a wide shallow beam is no less slender than a narrow shallow one.

questions.stem: Contour lines of different elevations can unite to form one line only in case of:
questions.solution:
**A vertical cliff.**

Contours of different elevation normally cannot meet, because a single point on the ground has one and only one elevation. The **vertical cliff** is the sole exception: there, several elevations lie **directly above one another** in plan, so their contours coincide and appear as a single line.

The properties of contour lines, which this question tests one of:

| Property | Note |
|---|---|
| Two contours of different elevation **cannot cross** | Except an **overhanging cliff**, where they cross |
| Contours of different elevation **cannot unite** | Except a **vertical cliff**, where they coincide |
| Contours **close on themselves**, within or beyond the map | A closed contour is a hill or a depression |
| Closed contours with **higher** values inside | **Hill or summit** |
| Closed contours with **lower** values inside | **Depression, pond or pit** |
| Contours cross a **ridge or valley line at right angles** | Ridge: convex towards lower ground; valley: convex towards higher |
| **Closely spaced** contours | **Steep** slope |
| **Widely spaced** contours | **Gentle** slope |
| Equally spaced contours | Uniform slope |

Note the pair of exceptions and keep them apart: a **vertical** cliff makes contours **unite**; an **overhanging** cliff makes them **cross**. Both are the only cases in which the general rules are broken.

Why the other options fail: a **saddle** (b) is a col or pass between two summits, shown by two sets of closed contours meeting in a figure-of-eight — the contours do not unite. A **watershed line** (c) is a ridge line, crossed by contours at right angles. A **hill top** (d) is shown by closed contours with rising values inward.

**What contours are used for**, which is why the properties are examined:
- Determining **elevations and slopes** at any point.
- Drawing a **longitudinal section and profile** along a proposed alignment.
- Computing **earthwork volumes** and reservoir capacity, by measuring the area enclosed by successive contours and applying the trapezoidal or prismoidal rule.
- Locating an alignment at a chosen **grade** — a contour road follows a single contour, and a ruling gradient is set out by stepping a fixed distance between successive contours.
- Fixing the **catchment boundary** of a stream, by tracing the ridge lines.

The **contour interval** is chosen from the scale, the terrain and the purpose: small (0.5 to 1 m) for flat ground and detailed work, large (5 to 25 m) for hilly terrain and small-scale maps.

examTip.trap: **Unite** (coincide) and **cross** are different words describing different features, and the question hinges on which is being asked.
examTip.trick: A **vertical cliff** makes contours **coincide** — several elevations at the same plan position. An **overhanging cliff** makes them **CROSS** — the surface doubles back over itself.
examTip.mnemonic: **Vertical cliff = contours UNITE. Overhang or cave = contours CROSS.** Otherwise contours never meet, because one point cannot have two surface elevations. Read the verb carefully.

questions.stem: The detention period in a septic tank is assumed:
questions.solution:
**24 hours.**

A septic tank is a watertight chamber for the on-site treatment of household sewage, and a detention period of about **24 hours** is provided so that the solids can settle and the retained sludge can undergo **anaerobic digestion**.

Standard design features (IS 2470):

| Feature | Value |
|---|---|
| **Detention time** | **24 hours** |
| Length : breadth | **2 : 1 to 4 : 1** |
| **Minimum width** | **750 mm** |
| Minimum liquid depth | 1.0 – 1.8 m |
| Free board | 300 mm |
| Compartments | **Two**, the first about ⅔ of the length |
| **Sludge removal interval** | **2 to 3 years** |
| Sludge allowance | ~30 L per person per year |

**How it works.** Sewage entering the tank separates into three layers: a floating **scum** of grease and light matter, a clear middle **liquid** zone, and a bottom **sludge** blanket. Anaerobic bacteria digest the sludge, reducing its volume and converting organics to methane, carbon dioxide and hydrogen sulphide, which are vented.

The **two-compartment** arrangement matters: most settlement occurs in the first chamber, and the second polishes the effluent and guards against carry-over if the first is disturbed. **Baffles or T-pipes** at inlet and outlet keep the scum from escaping.

**The critical limitation, and the commonest error in practice.** A septic tank removes only about **30 to 50% of BOD**. Its effluent is anaerobic, foul and still dangerous, and it **must** be followed by secondary disposal — a **soak pit, dispersion trench or leach field** — sized from the soil's percolation rate. Discharging septic tank effluent directly to a drain or watercourse is a public health hazard, and treating the tank as complete treatment is a frequent and serious mistake.

Septic tanks suit **unsewered areas** — much of Nepal outside the larger municipalities — and require permeable soil with the water table well below the disposal field. Where the ground is impermeable or the water table high, the effluent cannot soak away and the system fails.

Set 6 Q38 asks the same figure, and Set 3 Q64 the related activated-sludge parameter, the **sludge volume index**.

examTip.trick: A septic tank needs long enough for **solids to settle and anaerobic digestion to begin** — a day is the conventional domestic figure.
examTip.mnemonic: **Detention 24 hours; desludge every 1–2 years.** The critical point: the **effluent is NOT treated** — it still carries pathogens and BOD, so it must go to a **soak pit or drain field**, never to a watercourse. That second stage is the part most often omitted or undersized.

questions.stem: Pick up the correct statement from the following:
options: Failure plane carries maximum shear stress
Failure plane does not carry maximum shear stress
Failure plane carries shear stress equal to maximum shear stress
questions.solution:
**The failure plane does not carry the maximum shear stress.**

This is one of the most counter-intuitive results in soil mechanics, and it follows from the fact that **normal stress helps resist sliding**.

On the Mohr circle, the plane of maximum shear is at the **top** of the circle, at **45°** to the major principal plane. But failure occurs where the circle first **touches the Mohr–Coulomb envelope**

> τ = c + σ tan φ

and because that envelope **slopes upward** at angle φ, it touches the circle at a point *before* the top. The tangency point corresponds to a physical plane at

> **θ_f = 45° + φ/2**

not 45°.

| Plane | Inclination to major principal plane | On the Mohr circle |
|---|---|---|
| **Maximum shear stress** | **45°** | Top of the circle |
| **Failure plane** | **45° + φ/2** | Point of tangency with the envelope |

**Why the soil fails on the "wrong" plane.** The plane of maximum shear also carries a substantial normal stress, and that normal stress mobilises friction which resists sliding. A slightly differently inclined plane carries less shear but **much** less normal stress, so its ratio of driving to resisting stress is worse. Failure occurs on the plane where that ratio is **critical**, not where the shear stress alone is greatest.

**The important special case:** when **φ = 0** — a saturated clay tested undrained — the envelope is horizontal, tangency occurs at the top of the circle, and the failure plane *does* coincide with the plane of maximum shear at 45°. So the two planes agree only for a purely cohesive soil.

The relation at failure that follows from the geometry:

> σ₁ = σ₃ tan²(45° + φ/2) + 2c tan(45° + φ/2)

with tan²(45° + φ/2) = K_p, the passive earth pressure coefficient — which is why the same 45° + φ/2 angle appears in the Rankine failure wedge behind a retaining wall.

Contrast the situation in an **isotropic elastic material** (Set 4 Q30, Set 3 Q72): there a ductile metal *does* yield in shear on the 45° plane, giving the cup-and-cone fracture. The difference is that a metal's strength does not depend on the confining pressure, whereas a soil's does — and that pressure dependence is precisely what rotates the failure plane.

examTip.trick: The maximum shear plane is at **45°**, but the **failure** plane is at **45 + φ/2**. Soil does not fail where the shear is greatest, because the **normal stress there is higher** and supplies extra frictional resistance.
examTip.mnemonic: **Failure occurs where the ratio of shear to available strength is worst, not where shear is largest.** The two planes coincide only when **φ = 0** — saturated clay tested undrained. That single fact is the physical content of the Mohr–Coulomb envelope.

questions.stem: When the flow in an open channel is gradually varied, the flow is said to be:
questions.solution:
**Steady non-uniform flow.**

Two independent questions classify any flow, and the terms must be kept apart:

| Question | Answer | Term |
|---|---|---|
| Does the depth change **with time** at a point? | No | **Steady** |
| Does the depth change **with distance** along the channel? | Yes | **Non-uniform** (varied) |

In **gradually varied flow (GVF)** the depth changes along the channel — so the flow is **non-uniform** — but at any fixed location it does not change with time, so it is **steady**. Hence steady non-uniform flow.

The four combinations:

| Flow | Depth vs time | Depth vs distance | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Steady uniform | Constant | **Constant** | Long prismatic channel at **normal depth** |
| **Steady non-uniform** | Constant | **Varies** | **GVF** — backwater curve upstream of a weir; **RVF** — a hydraulic jump |
| Unsteady uniform | Varies | Constant | Practically non-existent |
| Unsteady non-uniform | Varies | Varies | **Flood wave** travelling down a river; surge |

**Gradually versus rapidly varied**, the sub-distinction within non-uniform flow:

| | **GVF** | **RVF** |
|---|---|---|
| Depth changes | **Gradually**, over a long distance | **Abruptly**, over a short distance |
| Streamline curvature | Negligible — pressure remains hydrostatic | Strong — pressure not hydrostatic |
| Energy loss | Friction only | **Significant local loss** |
| Examples | **Backwater** and drawdown curves | **Hydraulic jump**, flow over a weir, sluice gate |

That difference matters because the **hydrostatic pressure assumption** holds in GVF, which is what allows the governing equation to be written as

> **dy/dx = (S₀ − S_f)/(1 − Fr²)**

In RVF it does not, and momentum rather than energy must be used — which is why the hydraulic jump is analysed by the momentum equation and its energy loss computed afterwards.

**Where GVF arises in practice**, and why it is computed: a weir, dam or bridge constriction raises the water level upstream, and that **backwater curve** extends for a considerable distance — often kilometres on a mild slope. Determining how far the raised level reaches decides the extent of land submerged, the height of flood embankments, and the afflux at a bridge. The profiles are classified by the slope and the depth relative to normal and critical: **M1, M2, M3** on a mild slope, **S1, S2, S3** on a steep one.

examTip.trap: **Steady** and **uniform** are independent, and conflating them is the trap. **Steady is about TIME; uniform is about SPACE.**
examTip.trick: Gradually varied flow has a **constant discharge** (so nothing changes with time — steady) but a **depth that changes along the channel** (so it is non-uniform).
examTip.mnemonic: **Uniform flow = normal depth, surface parallel to the bed. GVF = backwater curves. RVF = hydraulic jump.** The GVF equation **dy/dx = (S₀ − S_f)/(1 − Fr²)** is singular at Fr = 1 — which is precisely why nature needs a jump there.

questions.stem: In a plastic analysis of structures, the segment between any two successive plastic hinges is assumed to deform as:
questions.solution:
**A rigid material.**

Plastic analysis assumes an **idealised rigid–plastic** material: no deformation at all until the plastic moment M_p is reached, then unlimited rotation at constant moment. Under that idealisation, all the deformation at collapse is **concentrated at the plastic hinges**, and the segments between them stay **straight and undeformed** — they simply rotate as rigid links.

That assumption is what makes the method work. Because the segments are rigid bars pinned at the hinges, the collapse mechanism is a **kinematic linkage**, and the collapse load follows from a simple work equation:

> **External work done by the loads = Internal work absorbed at the hinges**
> Σ(W · δ) = Σ(M_p · θ)

No integration and no elastic analysis is needed — only geometry.

**The idealisation compared with reality:**

| | Rigid–plastic idealisation | Real behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| Before M_p | **No deformation** | Elastic deformation throughout |
| At M_p | Hinge rotates freely | Yielding spreads over a finite **plastic hinge length** |
| Segments | **Rigid, straight** | Slightly curved (elastic) |

The elastic deformation neglected is small compared with the plastic rotation at collapse, so the error in the **collapse load** is negligible — which is why the method is accepted for design even though the assumption is plainly an approximation.

**Number of hinges needed.** A mechanism forms when

> **Number of plastic hinges = D_s + 1**

where D_s is the degree of static indeterminacy. So a **simply supported** beam (D_s = 0) needs **one** hinge; a **propped cantilever** (D_s = 1) needs **two** — at the fixed end and at 0.414L from the propped end, as computed in Set 1 Q23; a **fixed beam** (D_s = 3 for a plane member, but 2 hinges plus the mechanism in a single span) collapses with three.

**Why plastic analysis is worth doing.** It gives the **true collapse load**, which for an indeterminate structure is substantially higher than the load at first yield. As one section reaches M_p it stops taking more moment and **redistributes** the excess to its neighbours, so the structure carries on until enough hinges have formed to make a mechanism. Elastic design, which stops at first yield, therefore wastes that reserve.

The reserve is measured by the **shape factor** (M_p/M_y — 1.5 for a rectangle, 1.10–1.20 for a rolled I-beam, per Set 1 Q1) multiplied by the **redistribution** the indeterminacy allows. And it exists only because steel is **ductile** enough to rotate at the hinges without fracturing — which is why plastic design is permitted for steel but not for brittle materials, and why over-reinforced concrete sections, which fail without ductility, are prohibited.

examTip.trick: In plastic analysis, all the inelastic deformation is assumed to concentrate at **discrete plastic hinges**. Between hinges the member is treated as **rigid**, so the collapse mechanism is made of straight segments rotating about the hinges.
examTip.mnemonic: **Collapse load found by equating EXTERNAL work to INTERNAL work at the hinges.** The number of hinges to form a mechanism is **D_s + 1** — so a propped cantilever (D_s = 1) needs **two**, and a fixed beam (D_s = 3)... needs one per redundancy plus one.

questions.stem: The top soil of a water-logged field becomes more alkaline and infertile if its pH value is:
