questions.solution:
**11.**

A pH above about **11** renders soil practically infertile. The scale runs from acid through neutral to increasingly hostile alkalinity, and the thresholds matter:

| pH | Condition | Fertility |
|---|---|---|
| < 6 | Acidic | Poor; corrected with **lime** |
| **6.5 – 7.5** | **Near neutral** | **Best for most crops** |
| ~8.5 | **Saline** soil | Structure still good |
| 8.5 – 10 | Saline–sodic | Structure deteriorating |
| > 10 | **Sodic (alkali)** soil | Structureless |
| **> 11** | Strongly sodic | **Practically infertile** |

**Why high pH destroys fertility** — the mechanism is physical as much as chemical:

1. The high pH arises from **sodium carbonate**, which is highly soluble.
2. Excess **exchangeable sodium** on the clay causes the clay to **deflocculate and disperse** rather than remaining aggregated.
3. Dispersed clay **seals the pore structure**. The soil becomes almost impermeable, so water and air cannot move through it.
4. On drying, the surface forms a hard **crust**, which prevents seedlings from emerging.
5. Dissolved organic matter deposits a **black surface** on evaporation — the origin of the term "black alkali".
6. Chemically, high pH also locks up **phosphorus, iron, zinc and manganese**, making them unavailable to plants.

So the soil fails on structure, on aeration, on permeability and on nutrient availability simultaneously.

**The distinction that governs the remedy** is between saline and sodic soil, and it is examined constantly:

| | **Saline** | **Sodic (alkali)** |
|---|---|---|
| Problem | High **soluble salts** | High **exchangeable sodium** |
| ESP | < 15 | **> 15** |
| pH | 7.5 – 8.5 | **> 8.5** |
| Structure | Retained | **Destroyed** |
| **Remedy** | **Leaching** with drainage | **Gypsum or pyrite first**, then leach |

Leaching alone cannot help a sodic soil, because the soil is impermeable — water will not pass through it. **Gypsum (CaSO₄)** supplies calcium to replace sodium on the exchange sites, the clay reflocculates, permeability is restored, and only then can the displaced sodium sulphate be washed out. **Amend first, leach second** (Set 2 Q35).

**Why waterlogging causes it.** A high water table brings salts up by **capillary rise**; evaporation at the surface leaves them behind and concentrates them year on year. So the root cause is drainage, and the permanent cure is **lowering the water table** — surface and sub-surface drains, tube wells, and lining the canals whose seepage raised the table in the first place (Set 2 Q96, Set 3 Q46).

examTip.trick: **Alkali (sodic) soils** have pH above about **8.5**, and severely affected ones reach **10 or higher**. Above that the clay disperses, structure collapses and the soil becomes almost impermeable.
examTip.mnemonic: **Saline soil: high salts, pH below 8.5, treat by LEACHING. Alkali/sodic soil: high sodium, pH above 8.5, treat with GYPSUM then leach.** Gypsum supplies calcium to replace the sodium on the exchange sites — leaching alone would make a sodic soil worse.

questions.stem: The minimum radius of curvature for a hairpin bend in hill roads is:
questions.solution:
**15 m.**

A **hairpin bend** is the sharp reversal of direction used to gain height on a steep hillside where a straighter alignment would exceed the ruling gradient. Because the terrain leaves no room for a normal curve, the standards are relaxed — but not without limit.

The design parameters for hairpin bends under Nepal Road Standard 2070 (Table 9-3):

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| **Minimum design speed** | **20 km/h** |
| **Minimum radius of curvature** | **15 m** |
| **Minimum length of transition curve** | **15 m** |
| **Maximum longitudinal gradient** | **4%** |
| **Maximum superelevation** | **10%** |

Two of these deserve comment because they look surprising.

**Why the gradient is limited to 4%** — *lower* than the ruling gradient of about 5 to 7% used on the open hill road. On a very sharp curve the vehicle must also overcome **curve resistance**, and a long vehicle's rear wheels track a much tighter path. Combining a steep grade with a sharp curve would exceed what a loaded truck can climb, so the grade is **compensated** — flattened — through the bend. This is the general principle of **grade compensation** on curves, applied at its extreme.

**Why superelevation reaches 10%** — the maximum permitted anywhere. With R as small as 15 m, the centrifugal force is large even at 20 km/h, and the full available superelevation is needed to counter it.

A check on the numbers, using the standard curve relation:
> e + f = v²/(127R) = 20²/(127 × 15) = 400/1905 = **0.21**

With e = 0.10, the friction required is f = 0.11 — comfortably within the available lateral friction, so the combination is consistent.

**Design practice for hairpins**, beyond the table: they should be located on **stable ground with a gentle natural slope**, never on a spur nose or in a slide-prone gully; successive bends should be separated by a reasonable distance; **extra widening** is essential because of off-tracking on so small a radius; and full-width **drainage and slope protection** matter more here than anywhere, since the bend concentrates run-off.

For comparison, ordinary hill road curves use a minimum radius of about 20 to 50 m depending on the design speed, so 15 m is genuinely the floor — reserved for the hairpin case.

examTip.trick: A hairpin bend is a deliberate exception to the normal minimum radius, accepted because gaining height on a steep hillside leaves no alternative. It comes with compensating measures.
examTip.mnemonic: **A hairpin gets: minimum radius relaxed, but EXTRA WIDENING, a flatter gradient through the bend (about 2.5% maximum), full superelevation, and a minimum length of straight between successive bends.** The gradient compensation matters most — a steep grade on a tight curve is where trucks stall.

questions.stem: A moment M is acting at the centre of a cantilever beam of length L. What will be the value of shear force and bending moment at the fixed end?
questions.solution:
**Shear force 0, bending moment M.**

**Shear force.** A couple is a **self-equilibrating** pair of forces — its net force is zero. Taking any section and summing the vertical forces on one side, there is no transverse load anywhere on the beam, so

> **V = 0 at every section**, including the fixed end.

**Bending moment.** A couple transmits its full moment to any section **beyond** the point of application, undiminished by distance. Since the fixed end lies beyond the mid-point where M is applied:

> **M_fixed = M**

Between the free end and the mid-point there is nothing at all, so the moment there is **zero**.

The complete diagrams, which is the useful picture:

| Region | Shear force | Bending moment |
|---|---|---|
| Free end to mid-point | **0** | **0** |
| Mid-point to fixed end | **0** | **M** (constant) |

So the BM diagram is a **step** — zero over the outer half, jumping to M at the point of application and staying constant to the support. The **inner half is in pure bending**: constant moment, zero shear, uniform curvature.

**Why the moment does not vary with distance.** This is the point candidates most often get wrong. A **force** produces a moment that grows with the lever arm; a **couple** has no lever arm to grow — it is already a moment. Hence option (d), M/L, is dimensionally a force and cannot be a bending moment at all; and option (b) inverts the two answers.

Compare the two cantilever loadings side by side:

| Loading at free end | Shear force | Bending moment at fixed end |
|---|---|---|
| **Point load W** | **W** (constant) | **WL** — grows with span |
| **Moment M** | **0** | **M** — independent of span |

The deformations follow from the M/EI diagram, which here is a rectangle of area M·(L/2) over the inner half:

> Slope at free end θ = **ML/(2EI)**
> Deflection at free end δ = **3ML²/(8EI)**

Set 6 Q31 asks the companion question — a moment applied at the **free end** of a cantilever, where the moment is then constant at M along the *whole* beam.

examTip.trick: A couple applied at **mid-length** of a cantilever produces **zero moment on the free-end side** (nothing between there and the couple) and a **constant moment M** from the couple to the fixed end.
examTip.mnemonic: **A couple STEPS the bending moment diagram and leaves the shear untouched** — the exact reverse of a point load, which jumps the shear and only kinks the moment. That contrast is a standard examination discriminator.

questions.stem: The discharge passing through an ogee spillway is 90 m³/s. Calculate the length of crest if the head over the crest is 1.6 m. (Take value of C = 1.7)
questions.solution:
**26 m.**

**The weir formula:**
> Q = C · L · H^{3/2}

**Substituting Q = 90 m³/s, C = 1.7, H = 1.6 m:**
> 90 = 1.7 × L × 1.6^{1.5}

**Evaluating the power:**
> 1.6^{1.5} = 1.6 × √1.6 = 1.6 × 1.2649 = **2.0239**

**Solving for L:**
> 90 = 1.7 × L × 2.0239 = 3.4406 L
> L = 90/3.4406 = **26.16 m ≈ 26 m** ✓

The **3/2 power** is the essential feature and worth understanding rather than memorising. Discharge is velocity × area; over a weir the velocity scales as √H (from Torricelli) and the flow area also grows with H, so

> Q ∝ √H × H = **H^{3/2}**

That reasoning also gives the exponents for the other shapes:

| Device | Q proportional to |
|---|---|
| **Rectangular / broad-crested / ogee weir** | **H^{3/2}** |
| **Triangular (V-notch)** | **H^{5/2}** — the width grows with depth too |
| Orifice, siphon spillway (running full) | **H^{1/2}** — fixed area |

Set 6 Q36 is the companion question, where the circulating key wrongly gave √H for an ogee weir; the exponent is 3/2, as the arithmetic here confirms.

**The practical consequence of the 3/2 power** is that a **small rise in head passes a large increase in discharge** — which makes a weir both an effective flood-passing structure and a good flow-measuring device. Doubling the head here would pass 2^1.5 = 2.83 times the discharge.

**Design notes on the coefficient.** For an ogee spillway C is about **2.2 in SI units** at the design head; the value of 1.7 given here corresponds to a broad-crested condition, and in practice C varies with the crest shape, the approach velocity and the ratio H/H_d. The **ogee profile** itself is shaped to follow the lower nappe of a freely falling jet, so that at the design head the pressure along the crest is atmospheric — avoiding both the cavitation risk of negative pressure and the discharge reduction of positive pressure (Set 3 Q95).

Note also that H should strictly be the **total** head including the approach velocity head, H = H_static + v²/2g, though the velocity term is often negligible.

examTip.trick: **Q = C L H^(3/2)** for an ogee spillway, with C typically **2.2** in SI units. Rearrange for L, keeping H in metres.
examTip.mnemonic: **The ogee profile follows the LOWER NAPPE of a freely falling jet at the design head** — so the water just stays in contact and the crest pressure is near atmospheric. **At higher heads the flow tends to lift off, creating sub-atmospheric pressure and CAVITATION risk**, which is why the design head and the crest tolerances matter.

questions.stem: If the initial investment for a machine is Rs 10,000 and the depreciation amount per year is Rs 1,600, then calculate the book value at the end of 5 years.
questions.solution:
**Rs 2,000.**

With a **constant** annual depreciation the method is straight line, and the calculation is two steps:

**Step 1 — accumulated depreciation over 5 years:**
> D_total = 1,600 × 5 = **Rs 8,000**

**Step 2 — book value = initial cost − accumulated depreciation:**
> BV = 10,000 − 8,000 = **Rs 2,000** ✓

Note that option (d), Rs 8,000, is the **accumulated depreciation** itself — the trap for anyone who stops at step 1.

**Reading the numbers backwards** tells you the assumptions implied. Straight-line depreciation is

> D = (C − S)/n

so with D = 1,600 and C = 10,000, the machine has been depreciated over a life and salvage value satisfying (10,000 − S)/n = 1,600 — for instance a 5-year life with S = Rs 2,000, or a 6-year life with S = Rs 400. The book value at 5 years of Rs 2,000 is consistent with the first reading.

**The depreciation methods**, since the question turns on recognising which one applies:

| Method | Annual charge | Character |
|---|---|---|
| **Straight line** | **(C − S)/n — constant** | Simplest; used here |
| Declining balance | A **fixed percentage of the reducing book value** | Higher charge in early years |
| Sum-of-years-digits | Decreasing charge | Accelerated |
| Sinking fund | A uniform deposit accumulating to (C − S) | Includes interest earned |
| Production units | Charge per unit of output | Suits plant with variable use |

The **declining balance** methods write value off faster at the start, which better reflects how most plant actually loses market value, and they defer tax — which is why they are common in practice even though straight line is simpler.

**Why book value matters to the engineer**, not only the accountant. It is the figure used in **replacement analysis**: the decision whether to keep or replace a machine compares the **equivalent uniform annual cost** of retaining it (rising, as maintenance grows and the remaining value falls) against that of a new one. Note also the distinction from Set 3 Q53: **book value** is the accounting figure, **salvage value** is what the asset would fetch intact at the end of its life, and **scrap value** what its dismantled materials are worth. The three are routinely confused and rarely equal.

examTip.trick: **Straight line depreciation = (C − S)/n**, and with no salvage value stated it is simply C/n. Work backwards from the annual amount to whichever quantity is asked for.
examTip.mnemonic: **Straight line writes off an EQUAL AMOUNT each year; DECLINING BALANCE writes off a fixed PERCENTAGE**, so it depreciates faster early on — which is closer to how plant actually loses value. The **sinking fund** method is the third, accumulating a fund to replace the asset.

questions.stem: Two capillary tubes P and Q are dipped in water. The height of water level in capillary P is 2/3 of the height in capillary Q. The ratio of their diameters is:
questions.solution:
**3 : 2.**

**The governing relation.** Capillary rise:
> h = 4σ cos θ / (ρ g d)

Same liquid, same tube material, so σ, θ and ρ are fixed. Therefore

> **h ∝ 1/d**, or **h·d = constant**

**Applying it.** Given h_P = (2/3) h_Q:
> h_P · d_P = h_Q · d_Q
> (2/3) h_Q · d_P = h_Q · d_Q
> (2/3) d_P = d_Q

> **d_P : d_Q = 3 : 2** ✓

**The check that confirms the direction.** Tube P has the **lower** rise, so — since rise is inversely proportional to diameter — P must be the **wider** tube. The ratio d_P : d_Q must therefore exceed 1, and 3:2 = 1.5 does. Option (a), 2:3, is the same numbers inverted and is the trap for anyone who carries the 2/3 straight across.

That inverse-proportion sanity check is worth making a habit: **smaller tube, higher rise.**

**Why the rise happens at all.** Water **wets** glass (contact angle θ ≈ 0°), so adhesion between liquid and solid exceeds the liquid's own cohesion, the meniscus is concave, and surface tension pulls the column up. **Mercury** does the opposite: θ ≈ 130–140°, cos θ is negative, the meniscus is convex, and the liquid is **depressed** — the case worked in Set 2 Q65.

| Liquid in glass | Contact angle | Meniscus | Effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Water** | ≈ 0° | Concave | **Rise** |
| **Mercury** | ≈ 130–140° | Convex | **Depression** |

**Where the 1/d law matters in engineering:**
- **Manometer and piezometer tubes** are kept above about **6 mm** bore so the capillary correction can be ignored — below that the error becomes significant.
- **Capillary rise in soils** follows the same law with the pore size in place of d, which is why fine silts draw water far higher than coarse sands, and why capillary rise governs **frost heave** and the depth at which a damp proof course is needed.
- It also explains why **fine-grained soils** retain moisture against gravity — the capillary water that is the plant's usable supply (Set 3 Q15).

examTip.trick: **h = 4σcosθ/(γd)**, so **h ∝ 1/d**. The heights are in the **inverse ratio of the diameters** — so a height ratio of 3:2 means a diameter ratio of 2:3.
examTip.mnemonic: **Fine tube, high rise — inversely proportional.** In soils the same relation explains why **silt** has such a large capillary rise (1–10 m) and why silt is therefore the most **frost-susceptible** soil: it has both the rise and enough permeability to feed a growing ice lens.

questions.stem: The value of hydraulic radius in the most economical triangular channel is:
questions.solution:
**y/(2√2).**

**The most economical triangular section** has each sloping side inclined at **45° to the vertical** — that is, a side slope of 1H : 1V, making the total apex angle 90°.

**Deriving R for that section**, with y the depth:

> Top width T = 2y (each side extends y horizontally for depth y)
> **Area** A = ½ × T × y = ½ × 2y × y = **y²**
> **Wetted perimeter** P = 2 × y√2 = **2√2 y** (each sloping side has length y√2)

> **R = A/P = y²/(2√2 y) = y/(2√2)** ✓

Numerically R = 0.354 y.

**Why 45° is optimal.** A section is most economical when, for a given area, the **wetted perimeter is a minimum** — least friction, so maximum discharge, and least lining to pay for. Minimising P for fixed A in a triangle yields side slopes at 45°.

The most economical conditions for all the standard shapes, which should be learned together:

| Section | Most economical condition | Hydraulic radius |
|---|---|---|
| **Rectangle** | b = 2y | **R = y/2** |
| **Trapezoid** | Top width = 2 × sloping side; best side slope 60° (half-hexagon) | **R = y/2** |
| **Triangle** | **Sides at 45° to vertical** | **R = y/(2√2)** |
| Circle (max velocity) | y = 0.81 D | R = 0.3 D |
| Circle (max discharge) | y = 0.95 D | — |

Note that **R = y/2 is common to the rectangle and the trapezoid** — worth remembering as a single fact — and that the triangle is the exception, which is exactly why it is asked. Option (a), y/2, is the trap for a candidate who recalls the common case without noticing the shape.

**Why it matters.** Through Manning's equation,

> V = (1/n) R^{2/3} S^{1/2},  Q = A V

the hydraulic radius controls the discharge a section can carry. Maximising R for a given area is therefore the same thing as maximising capacity — and minimising the lining area, which is the cost. The trapezoidal section dominates real canal design because it combines near-optimal hydraulics with **stable side slopes** in earth; a true 45° triangular channel would be efficient hydraulically but is used mainly for small lined drains and roadside channels, since the slopes are too steep for most soils to hold.

examTip.trick: For the most economical triangular channel the side slopes are at **45°**, and working through A/P gives **R = y/(2√2)**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Economical sections: rectangle b = 2y (R = y/2); trapezoid 60° sides, half a hexagon (R = y/2); triangle 45° sides (R = y/2√2); semicircle (R = y/2).** Three of the four give **R = y/2** — the triangle is the exception, and that is what makes it the memorable one.

questions.stem: The horizontal thrust in a two hinged semi-circular arch subjected to UDL of w kN/m over the left half span will be:
questions.solution:
**2wR/3π.**

**The standard result for full loading.** For a two-hinged semicircular arch of radius R carrying a UDL of w over the **entire** span:

> H = **4wR/(3π)**

**Half loading.** The horizontal thrust is obtained from

> H = ∫(M y ds/EI) / ∫(y² ds/EI)

The denominator depends only on the **geometry** and is unchanged. The numerator is **linear in the applied loading**, so loading only half the span produces exactly **half** the thrust:

> H = ½ × 4wR/(3π) = **2wR/(3π)** ✓

That linearity is the whole shortcut, and it is worth recognising: because the compatibility equation for a two-hinged arch is linear in the load, **superposition applies**. Half the load gives half the thrust; two separate loads give the sum of their individual thrusts.

**A useful sanity check on the options.** Dimensionally, w [kN/m] × R [m] = kN, so every option is dimensionally a force — the distinction has to be made on magnitude. Numerically 4/(3π) = 0.42 and 2/(3π) = 0.21, so full loading gives H ≈ 0.42wR and half loading ≈ 0.21wR. Options (b) wR/2 = 0.5wR and (c) wR are both larger than the *fully* loaded value, which is impossible for a partially loaded arch — so they can be eliminated on inspection.

**Two-hinged versus three-hinged**, the distinction this whole family of questions rests on:

| | **Two-hinged** | **Three-hinged** |
|---|---|---|
| Indeterminacy | **1 degree** | **0 — determinate** |
| H found from | **Compatibility**, ∂U/∂H = 0, needing EI | **Statics** — moments about the crown hinge |
| Formula | H = ∫(My ds/EI)/∫(y² ds/EI) | **H = M_c/y_c** |
| Sensitive to settlement, temperature | **Yes** — develops secondary stresses | **No** — free to adjust |

So the three-hinged arch is far easier to analyse (Set 2 Q62 took three lines of statics) but the two-hinged arch is stiffer and more commonly built.

**The general lesson about arch action**, from H = M_c/y_c: the thrust is **inversely proportional to the rise**. A shallow arch develops enormous horizontal thrust, which the abutments must resist — which is why flat arches need massive foundations or a tie rod, and why the arch form suits a **narrow gorge with sound rock** abutments above all.

examTip.trick: A two-hinged arch is **indeterminate to degree 1**, so the thrust comes from strain energy: **H = ∫My ds/EI ÷ ∫y² ds/EI**, evaluated for the semicircular geometry.
examTip.mnemonic: **Two-hinged: indeterminate, needs strain energy. THREE-hinged: DETERMINATE** — the crown hinge gives H = M_crown/rise by statics alone. That is why three-hinged arches are chosen where **settlement or temperature movement** is expected: being determinate, they develop no self-stress.

questions.stem: The bearing capacity of soft clay in kPa is:
questions.solution:
**About 50 kPa.**

Soft clay has a high natural water content, a high void ratio and very low shear strength, so its safe bearing capacity is at the bottom of the range for any soil — around **50 kN/m²**.

The presumptive safe bearing capacities of IS 1904, which are worth carrying as an order-of-magnitude check:

| Soil | Safe bearing capacity (kPa) |
|---|---|
| **Soft clay** | **50** |
| Medium clay | 100 – 150 |
| Stiff clay | 150 – 250 |
| Hard clay | 250 – 450 |
| Loose sand | 100 – 150 |
| Medium sand | 150 – 250 |
| Dense sand / gravel | 250 – 450 |
| Soft rock | 450 |
| **Hard rock** | **3000 – 4000** |

So soft clay is roughly **sixty times weaker** than sound rock, which is why the choice of foundation type is so strongly governed by the ground.

**Where the figure comes from theoretically.** For a saturated clay loaded undrained, φ = 0 and Terzaghi's expression collapses to

> q_nu = **5.7 c_u**

With a soft clay of c_u ≈ 25 kPa this gives q_nu ≈ 143 kPa, and applying the usual **factor of safety of about 3** yields a safe value near **50 kPa** — consistent with the table.

Note too the distinctive feature of the φ = 0 case: q_u depends on **c_u alone and not on the footing width**, which is quite unlike a sand where the 0.5γBN_γ term dominates.

**Why the presumptive values are only a starting point.** IS 1904 permits them for preliminary sizing, but a real design requires site testing, because two further considerations frequently govern in clay:

1. **Settlement, not strength, usually controls.** Clay consolidates slowly and by large amounts, so the **allowable** bearing pressure is often the value that keeps settlement within limits rather than the value the strength permits.
2. **Strength falls when wet.** As Q16 of this paper noted, cohesive soil loses shear strength on wetting, so the design value must reflect the worst moisture condition.

**The engineering response to soft clay** is therefore one of: a **raft** to spread the load and even out differential settlement (Set 3 Q12); **piles** taken through the soft layer to a competent stratum; **ground improvement** by preloading with sand or wick drains to accelerate consolidation before construction; or a **compensated (floating) foundation**, where the weight of excavated soil offsets the building weight so the net pressure increase is near zero.

examTip.trick: Presumptive bearing values by soil description (IS 1904): **soft clay 100 kPa** or less, **medium clay 245**, **stiff clay 440**, **loose sand 100**, **dense sand 440**, **hard rock 3300+**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Presumptive values are for PRELIMINARY sizing and as a SANITY CHECK — never for final design.** They ignore footing width, depth, water table, layering and settlement, which are precisely the factors that govern. But if your calculation gives 800 kPa on soft clay, the presumptive value is what tells you something is wrong.

questions.stem: In an infinite slope, FOS = 1.5 and angle of internal friction = 36°. Find the safe slope angle in degrees.
questions.solution:
**26°.**

For an infinite slope in a **cohesionless** soil (c′ = 0), dry, the factor of safety is

> **FoS = tan φ′ / tan β**

where β is the slope angle. Rearranging for the safe slope:

> **tan β = tan φ′ / FoS**

**Substituting:**
> tan β = tan 36° / 1.5
> tan β = 0.7265 / 1.5 = **0.4843**
> β = **25.84° ≈ 26°** ✓

**The physical reading.** With FoS = 1, β = φ′ = 36° — the **critical slope angle**, at which the slope is on the point of failure. This is the **angle of repose**: a dry granular material tipped into a heap stands at exactly φ′. Demanding a factor of safety of 1.5 flattens the safe slope to 26°.

Note the striking simplicity of the result: for a cohesionless infinite slope the factor of safety depends **only on φ′ and β** — it is **independent of the depth** of the potential failure surface and of the unit weight. So the slope is equally at risk at any depth, and its stability is a matter of geometry alone.

**The seepage case**, which is the one that governs in practice. With steady seepage parallel to the slope and the water table at the surface:

> FoS = (γ′/γ_sat) × (tan φ′ / tan β)

and with typical values γ_sat ≈ 20 kN/m³, γ′ ≈ 10.2 kN/m³, the ratio γ′/γ_sat ≈ **0.51**. The factor of safety is therefore **roughly halved** by saturation (Set 2 Q45).

Applying that here: a slope cut at 26° with FoS = 1.5 in the dry would fall to FoS ≈ **0.77** under full seepage — that is, it would **fail**. Designing a slope on dry-season parameters and then letting the monsoon saturate it is precisely the mechanism behind most landslides on Nepal's hill roads.

**Hence the design response:**
- Use **γ′/γ_sat** in the calculation wherever seepage can occur, or design for the saturated condition outright.
- Concentrate on **drainage** — surface drains, cut-off drains above the cut, sub-surface drains, weep holes in walls — since removing the water restores most of the strength.
- Note that a **breast wall or pitching without drainage can make matters worse** (Q52 of this paper), by trapping water in the slope while adding weight.

For a slope in **cohesive** soil the analysis is different: cohesion contributes strength independent of depth, so a **critical height** exists, given by H_c = 4c/(γ · S_n) via Taylor's stability number, and the failure surface is curved rather than plane.

examTip.trick: For an infinite slope in **dry cohesionless** soil, **F = tan φ/tan β**. Rearranged: **tan β = tan φ/F = tan 36°/1.5 = 0.7265/1.5 = 0.484**, giving **β = 25.8° ≈ 26°** ✓
examTip.mnemonic: **The HEIGHT cancels out entirely — a dry sand slope is stable at β < φ whatever its height.** Add **steady seepage** parallel to the slope and F is roughly **HALVED** (γ′/γ_sat ≈ 0.5), which is exactly why sand slopes stand all dry season and fail in the monsoon.

questions.stem: If CBR = 5%, then the resilient modulus as per NRS is:
questions.solution:
**50 MPa.**

The **resilient modulus** M_R is the elastic modulus of the subgrade under repeated (traffic) loading, and it is correlated to the CBR by two expressions depending on the CBR value:

| Condition | Correlation |
|---|---|
| **CBR ≤ 5%** | **M_R = 10 × CBR** (MPa) |
| CBR > 5% | M_R = 17.6 × CBR^{0.64} (MPa) |

**Substituting CBR = 5%**, which falls on the boundary and so uses the first expression:

> M_R = 10 × 5 = **50 MPa** ✓

A useful check: the second formula at CBR = 5 gives 17.6 × 5^{0.64} = 17.6 × 2.72 = 47.9 MPa — close to 50, as it must be, since the two expressions are constructed to meet at the changeover point.

**Why M_R rather than CBR.** The CBR test is a **static punching** test, and its result is an empirical index rather than a material property. Mechanistic-empirical pavement design instead needs a genuine **elastic modulus** to compute the stresses and strains in the layered system — the two critical ones being:

> **Vertical compressive strain** at the top of the subgrade → controls **rutting**
> **Horizontal tensile strain** at the bottom of the bituminous layer → controls **fatigue cracking**

The correlation above lets a designer obtain M_R from the CBR test that laboratories already run routinely, without needing repeated-load triaxial equipment.

**Where it sits in the design chain**, which is worth seeing whole:

> Subgrade **CBR** (soaked, 4 days) → **M_R** → layered elastic analysis → strains → pavement composition

alongside the traffic input:

> Commercial vehicles per day → **CSA** = 365·A·[(1+r)ⁿ−1]/r · **F** · **D**

where F is the vehicle damage factor and D the **lane distribution factor** (0.4 for a four-lane single carriageway, Set 3 Q68). The pavement is then selected from the IRC 37 or DoR catalogue for that combination of M_R and CSA.

**A practical note on the CBR value itself.** It must be the **soaked** CBR — four days' immersion — because the monsoon saturates the subgrade and that is the condition the pavement must survive. A design based on a dry-season CBR will over-estimate the subgrade support, and the pavement will rut in its first wet season.

examTip.trick: The standard correlation is **M_R = 10 × CBR (MPa)** for CBR up to about 5%, so 5% gives **50 MPa**.
examTip.mnemonic: **M_R ≈ 10 CBR in MPa** (or 1500 CBR in psi). CBR is a crude penetration index and the resilient modulus is a genuine stiffness — the correlation is convenient rather than fundamental, and it degrades badly above CBR 10, where more sophisticated testing is warranted.

questions.stem: What is the fire demand of a city of 1 lakh population by Buston's formula?
questions.solution:
**56,630 litres/minute.**

**Buston's formula:**
> Q = 5663 √P,  with **P in thousands** and Q in litres/minute

**Substituting P = 1 lakh = 100,000 = 100 thousand:**
> Q = 5663 × √100
> Q = 5663 × 10 = **56,630 l/min** ✓

In other units that is 944 l/s, or about 81.6 million litres per day if it were sustained — which of course it is not.

**The trap is the units of P.** Forgetting that P is in *thousands* and substituting 100,000 directly gives √100,000 = 316, and Q = 1,790,000 l/min — an absurd figure, but exactly the kind of error the distractors are built around. Note also that option (a) is the formula's constant itself, which is what you get if you forget to take the square root at all.

The fire demand formulae, all with **P in thousands** and Q in litres per minute:

| Formula | Expression | Q for P = 100 |
|---|---|---|
| **Kuchling's** | **3182 √P** | 31,820 l/min (530 l/s) |
| **Buston's** | **5663 √P** | **56,630 l/min** |
| Freeman's | 1136 [P/5 + 10] | 34,080 l/min |
| National Board (USA) | 4637 √P (1 − 0.01√P) | 41,733 l/min |

They differ by nearly a factor of two, which reflects that fire demand is a matter of policy and risk tolerance as much as calculation. Buston's is the most conservative of these. Set 1 Q70 asks the same population using **Kuchling's** formula, giving 530 l/s.

**How fire demand enters design**, which is the point of computing it:
- It is a **short-duration, very high-rate** requirement — hours, not days — so the annual *volume* it represents is trivial.
- But the **rate** governs the sizing of **distribution mains** and the **fire reserve** in the service reservoir, because the network must deliver it at adequate pressure while normal supply continues.
- It is therefore added to the **maximum daily demand** when sizing mains, and provided for as a distinct component of reservoir storage alongside the balancing and breakdown reserves (Set 2 Q40).
- Hydrants are spaced about 100 to 150 m apart, and a residual pressure of roughly 100 to 150 kPa must remain at the hydrant during the draw.

That combination — a large flow required occasionally, at pressure, anywhere in the network — is also the strongest argument for a **grid iron** layout, since water can then reach any hydrant from several directions (Set 3 Q90).

examTip.trick: **Buston's formula: Q = 5663√P** litres/min, with P in thousands. For P = 100: **5663 × 10 = 56 630 l/min** ✓
examTip.mnemonic: **Every fire-demand formula goes as √P — Kuchling (3182√P), Buston (5663√P), Freeman, and the National Board.** The square root is because fire risk scales with **built area**, not linearly with people. Fire demand is a **short-duration peak** that sizes the mains and the storage, never the treatment works.

questions.stem: The waterway for a bridge on a river in an alluvial plain having a dominant discharge of 3600 cumecs should be:
questions.solution:
**285 m.**

**Lacey's regime perimeter** gives the stable waterway a river in alluvium will adopt:

> **P = 4.75 √Q**

**Substituting Q = 3600 cumecs:**
> P = 4.75 × √3600
> P = 4.75 × 60 = **285 m** ✓

The numbers are chosen so that √3600 = 60 exactly, which makes the arithmetic clean — a hint that Lacey's formula is the intended route.

**Note the discharge used: the dominant discharge**, not the maximum flood. The dominant (channel-forming) discharge is the flow that does the most cumulative work in shaping the channel — big enough to move sediment, frequent enough to do so repeatedly — commonly the bankfull flow with a return period of 1 to 2 years, or roughly half to two-thirds of the maximum flood (Set 3 Q76). Using the extreme flood here would predict a channel far wider than the river actually maintains.

**Why the regime width is the right design width.** Depart from it in either direction and the river objects:

| Waterway provided | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **Narrower** than regime | **Afflux** — raised upstream level, more flooding; higher velocity and **deeper scour** at piers |
| **Wider** than regime | River **meanders within the structure**; shoaling, oblique approach flow, attack on one abutment |

The practical rule, from Set 2 Q74: adopt the **lesser** of Lacey's P and the actual bank-to-bank width — you cannot build wider than the valley, and there is no benefit in building wider than regime.

**What follows from the waterway**, in the design sequence:

> **Scour depth:** R = 0.47 (Q/f)^{1/3}, or **1.35(q²/f)^{1/3}** per unit width (Q75 of this paper)
> **Foundation level:** set below the anticipated scour, taken as a multiple of R depending on location — deepest at the guide bank nose and at the piers
> **Guide banks:** upstream 1.0–1.5 L, downstream 0.2–0.4 L, with a **launching apron** sized from the scour depth (Q47 of this paper)

The whole family of Lacey relations, for reference:

| Quantity | Expression |
|---|---|
| Silt factor | f = 1.76 √d (d in mm) |
| **Regime perimeter** | **P = 4.75 √Q** |
| Regime scour depth | R = 0.47 (Q/f)^{1/3} |
| Regime slope | S = f^{5/3}/(3340 Q^{1/6}) |

These apply only where the channel has attained **regime** — flowing in incoherent alluvium of the same grade as the material it transports. On a rocky bed or in a lined channel they do not apply.

examTip.trick: **Lacey's regime perimeter P = 4.75√Q** gives the stable waterway width for an alluvial river.
examTip.mnemonic: **P = 4.75√Q — the width a stable alluvial river naturally adopts for that discharge.** Constricting a river below its regime width forces **deeper scour**, which is why bridge and barrage waterways are set from this formula rather than from the bank-to-bank width. Then **grip length = R/3 BELOW maximum scour**.

questions.stem: If 'a' is the base amount of expenditure and 'b' is the increase in the operation cost each year over a period of 'n' years, the total cost of maintenance is:
questions.solution:
**a + (n − 1)b.**

This is a **uniform gradient (arithmetic) series**. The base amount a applies in the first year, and the increment b is added in every year *after* the first:

| Year | Cost |
|---|---|
| 1 | a |
| 2 | a + b |
| 3 | a + 2b |
| … | … |
| **n** | **a + (n − 1)b** |

So the cost in the nth year is **a + (n − 1)b**.

**The check that settles it in seconds.** Substitute **n = 1**. In the first year no increase has yet occurred, so the cost must be exactly a:

| Option | Value at n = 1 | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| (a) a + (n+1)b | a + 2b | ✗ |
| **(b) a + (n−1)b** | **a** | **✓** |
| (c) a × (n−1)b | 0 | ✗ — and dimensionally nonsense |
| (d) a − (n−1)b | a | ✓ at n = 1, but then **decreases** — contradicts "increase" |

Only (b) passes both tests: it gives a at n = 1 **and** increases with n. That habit of testing a formula at its simplest case is worth carrying into the exam — it resolves most "which expression" questions faster than deriving them.

Set 4 Q54 asks this identical question, which is a useful reminder that the papers repeat material across sittings.

**Where the gradient series is used.** Maintenance and operating costs typically rise year on year — plant ages, efficiency falls, repairs grow — so the gradient series models them better than a uniform annual figure. To bring the stream to a single comparable value:

> **Present worth:** P = A(P/A, i, n) + G(P/G, i, n)
> **Equivalent uniform annual cost:** A_eq = A + G(A/G, i, n)

where A is the base amount and G the gradient.

That equivalent annual cost is precisely what a **replacement analysis** needs: the EUAC of keeping an ageing machine **rises** as maintenance grows and its remaining value falls, while the EUAC of a new machine is constant. The economic life is the year in which the two cross — which is the practical reason this apparently trivial algebra matters.

examTip.trick: An **arithmetic gradient**: the cost rises by a fixed amount b each period. After the first period there have been **(n − 1)** increases, so the nth-year cost is **a + (n − 1)b**.
examTip.mnemonic: **The FIRST year has no increase yet** — that is where the −1 comes from, and where the mark is lost. Contrast a **geometric** gradient, where the cost is **multiplied** by (1 + g) each year rather than added to.

questions.stem: The total value of extra widening required at a horizontal curve on a two lane hill road of radius 42 m for a design speed of 50 kmph and for vehicles with wheel base 6 m is:
questions.solution:
**1.669 m.**

Extra widening is the sum of two independent components:

> **W_e = W_m + W_ps**

**Mechanical widening** — accounts for **off-tracking**, the rear wheels following a tighter radius than the front:
> W_m = n l²/(2R)
> W_m = (2 × 6²)/(2 × 42) = 72/84 = **0.857 m**

**Psychological widening** — accounts for drivers keeping further from the edge and from oncoming vehicles on a curve:
> W_ps = V/(9.5 √R)
> W_ps = 50/(9.5 × √42) = 50/(9.5 × 6.481) = 50/61.57 = **0.812 m**

**Total:**
> W_e = 0.857 + 0.812 = **1.669 m** ✓

Note how the distractors are constructed: **0.500 m** and **0.589 m** are near one or other component alone, and **0.669 m** differs from the answer only in its leading digit. Computing just one component, or dropping the number of lanes, lands on a plausible-looking wrong option — so both terms must be carried through.

**What each term depends on**, which is the conceptual content:

| Component | Depends on | Independent of |
|---|---|---|
| **Mechanical** W_m = nl²/2R | **Wheelbase** and number of lanes | Speed |
| **Psychological** W_ps = V/(9.5√R) | **Speed** | Wheelbase |

So one is a matter of **vehicle geometry** and the other of **driver behaviour** — genuinely separate effects, which is why they are added rather than one being taken as a proxy for the other (Set 3 Q44).

**Practical points:**
- Both terms vary as 1/R or 1/√R, so extra widening matters on **sharp** curves and becomes negligible on flat ones. IRC requires it only for radii below about 300 m.
- On a **single-lane** road the psychological term is omitted, since there is no oncoming vehicle in the same carriageway.
- The widening is introduced **progressively along the transition curve**, reaching its full value at the start of the circular arc — applied on the inner edge, or split between both.
- A wheelbase of 6 m corresponds to a **truck**, the standard design vehicle; IRC commonly uses 6.1 m.

On a hill road with R = 42 m, an extra 1.67 m on a two-lane carriageway is a substantial addition — roughly a quarter of the 7.0 m standard width — which is why hairpin bends and sharp hill curves look so much wider than the straights approaching them.

examTip.trick: **W_e = nl²/(2R) + V/(9.5√R)** — mechanical plus psychological. Both terms grow as R falls, and both must be included.
examTip.mnemonic: **Mechanical widening (nl²/2R) because rear wheels track INSIDE the front wheels; psychological (V/9.5√R) because drivers keep further from the edge on a curve.** On tight hill-road curves the total can exceed a metre and a half per lane — which is why hairpin bends look so much wider than the straight.

questions.stem: If a power station supplies 1000 MWh of electricity to its consumers for a period of two months, then the average demand during the period will be:
questions.solution:
**0.694 MW.**

**Average demand** is simply the energy supplied divided by the time over which it was supplied:

> **Average demand = Energy / Time**

**Step 1 — the period in hours.** Taking two months as 60 days:
> t = 60 × 24 = **1440 hours**

**Step 2 — divide:**
> Average demand = 1000 MWh / 1440 h = **0.694 MW**

Equivalently 694 kW.

**Reading the distractors** is instructive, because each corresponds to a specific slip:
- **1.39 MW** results from using **30 days** (720 hours) — one month instead of two.
- **0.694 kW** and **1.39 kW** come from a factor-of-1000 unit error.

So the two things to get right are the **period** and the **units** — the arithmetic itself is a single division.

**Where average demand fits among the power-system quantities**, which is the reason it is asked:

| Quantity | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Average demand** | **Energy supplied ÷ time** |
| Peak (maximum) demand | The highest demand recorded in the period |
| **Load factor** | **Average demand ÷ peak demand** |
| **Capacity factor** | **Average demand ÷ installed capacity** |
| Utilisation factor | Peak demand ÷ installed capacity |
| Demand factor | Peak demand ÷ connected load |

Average demand is therefore the numerator of both the **load factor** and the **capacity factor**, which is what makes it the pivotal figure: it converts an energy total into a power rating that can be compared with the plant's capability.

**Why the distinction matters commercially.** Energy (MWh) and capacity (MW) are **different commodities**, priced and contracted separately. A plant is paid for the energy it delivers but must be built to meet the **peak**, so the ratio between them — the load factor — largely determines whether it is economic. A low load factor means expensive plant standing idle much of the time.

For Nepal this is the central issue of hydropower economics: a **run-of-river** scheme has a low capacity factor (often 40 to 60%) because dry-season flows are a fraction of monsoon flows, so its annual energy is far below what the nameplate rating suggests. Set 2 Q68 works the calculation in the other direction — 84 GW at a 60% load factor yielding 441 TWh a year.

examTip.trick: **Average load = energy ÷ time.** Convert consistently: 1000 MWh over the stated period in hours gives the average load in MW.
examTip.mnemonic: **Load factor = average load ÷ MAXIMUM DEMAND (how evenly). Capacity factor = average load ÷ INSTALLED CAPACITY (how fully).** Both ≤ 1. **Diversity factor** is the odd one — sum of individual maxima ÷ system maximum, always **> 1**, because consumers do not all peak together.

questions.stem: Lacey's scour depth for a stream carrying a discharge of 3 cumecs per metre width having a silt factor 1.2 is:
questions.solution:
**2.64 m.**

**Lacey's scour depth per unit width:**
> **R = 1.35 (q²/f)^{1/3}**

where q is the discharge **per metre width** and f the silt factor.

**Substituting q = 3 m³/s/m and f = 1.2:**
> q² = 9
> q²/f = 9/1.2 = **7.5**
> (7.5)^{1/3} = **1.957**
> R = 1.35 × 1.957 = **2.64 m** ✓

**Which formula to use** is the first decision, and it depends on how the discharge is given:

| Discharge given as | Formula |
|---|---|
| **Total** discharge Q (cumecs) | R = **0.47 (Q/f)^{1/3}** |
| **Per unit width** q (cumecs/m) | R = **1.35 (q²/f)^{1/3}** |

The question specifies "per metre width", so the second applies. Using the first with q = 3 would give 0.47(2.5)^{1/3} = 0.64 m — badly wrong, and the commonest error here.

**The silt factor** comes from the bed material:
> f = 1.76 √d,  with d the mean particle size in **mm**

So f = 1.2 corresponds to d ≈ 0.46 mm — a medium sand, typical of an alluvial bed.

**Why scour depth is the critical output.** It fixes how deep the foundations must go:

| Location | Design scour depth |
|---|---|
| Straight reach | 1.25 R |
| Moderate bend | 1.5 R |
| Severe bend | 1.75 R |
| **Nose of a pier** | **2.0 R** |
| **Nose of a guide bank** | **2.0 – 2.5 R** |

Foundations are then taken a further margin below that level. **Scour is the leading cause of bridge failure** in alluvial rivers — the river digs beneath a pier during a flood and the pier settles or overturns, often with no prior warning. So this calculation is not academic: it determines whether the structure survives.

The **launching apron** at a guide bank toe (Set 2 Q34) is sized from the same figure: it must contain enough stone to armour the face of the scour hole as the apron launches down it, at a slope of about 2H : 1V.

The rest of the Lacey family, for reference: **P = 4.75√Q** for the regime waterway (Q71 of this paper), and **S = f^{5/3}/(3340 Q^{1/6})** for the regime slope (Set 3 Q62).

examTip.trick: **Lacey's normal scour depth R = 1.35(q²/f)^(1/3)** for discharge per unit width q, with **f = 1.76√d**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Then multiply R by the location factor: 1.25 straight reach, 1.75–2.0 severe bend, and 2.0 at a BRIDGE PIER NOSE.** Scour is usually what fixes the foundation depth near any watercourse — deeper than bearing capacity or frost would ever require.

questions.stem: The moisture content of a sludge is reduced from 90% to 80% in a sludge digestion tank. The percentage decrease in the volume of sludge is:
questions.solution:
**50%.**

**The governing relation.** The mass of **dry solids** is unchanged by digestion — only water leaves. So the volume varies inversely with the solids fraction:

> **V₂/V₁ = (100 − P₁)/(100 − P₂)**

where P is the moisture content as a percentage.

**Substituting P₁ = 90%, P₂ = 80%:**
> V₂/V₁ = (100 − 90)/(100 − 80) = 10/20 = **0.5**

**Percentage decrease:**
> (1 − 0.5) × 100 = **50%** ✓

**Why the answer is so much larger than the 10-point change in moisture content suggests.** Look at what happens to the *solids*: at 90% moisture the sludge is **10% solids**; at 80% moisture it is **20% solids**. The solids concentration has **doubled**, so the same dry mass now occupies **half** the volume. Option (c), 10%, is the trap for anyone who reads the 10-point difference in moisture as the answer.

That non-linearity is the practical point. At high moisture contents, removing a modest amount of water produces a dramatic reduction in volume:

| Moisture | Solids | Relative volume |
|---|---|---|
| 95% | 5% | 4.0 |
| **90%** | **10%** | **2.0** |
| **80%** | **20%** | **1.0** |
| 70% | 30% | 0.67 |
| 60% | 40% | 0.50 |

So the early stages of dewatering are by far the most productive, and the returns diminish rapidly thereafter.

**Why it matters in practice.** Sludge handling and disposal is one of the largest costs in sewage treatment, and cost scales with **volume** — tanker journeys, drying bed area, landfill space. Halving the volume halves that cost, which is why the treatment train devotes so much effort to it:

> **Thickening** (gravity or flotation) → **Digestion** (anaerobic, reducing both volume and organic content) → **Dewatering** (drying beds, centrifuge, belt or filter press) → **Disposal** (landfill, agricultural use, incineration)

**Anaerobic digestion** does more than remove water: it destroys 40 to 60% of the volatile solids, stabilises the sludge so it no longer putrefies, kills many pathogens, and produces **biogas** (about 65% methane) that can be used to heat the digester itself or to generate power.

Related parameter from Set 3 Q64: the **sludge volume index**, SVI = settled volume (mL/L) ÷ solids (g/L), which measures how readily activated sludge settles — above about 150 mL/g indicates **bulking**.

examTip.trick: The **solids mass is unchanged**; only water is removed. So **V₂/V₁ = (100 − 90)/(100 − 80) = 10/20 = 0.5** — the volume **halves**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Work with the SOLIDS fraction, never the moisture fraction.** V₂/V₁ = (100 − p₁)/(100 − p₂). A small change in moisture content near 90% produces an enormous change in volume — which is exactly why **sludge dewatering** is the dominant cost in sludge handling.

questions.stem: What is the net section area of a steel plate 40 cm wide and 10 mm thick with one bolt, if the diameter of the bolt hole is 18 mm?
questions.solution:
**38.2 cm².**

**Step 1 — gross area of the plate:**
> A_g = width × thickness = 40 cm × 1.0 cm = **40 cm²**

(10 mm = 1.0 cm.)

**Step 2 — area removed by the bolt hole**, over the plate thickness:
> A_hole = 1.8 cm × 1.0 cm = **1.8 cm²**

**Step 3 — net section area:**
> A_n = 40 − 1.8 = **38.2 cm²** ✓

Equivalently 3820 mm². Options (c) and (d), quoted in mm², are an order of magnitude too small — a units trap.

**A note on the source working.** The circulating answer sheet keys (a), which is correct, but its arithmetic line reads *"Net area of plate 40 − 1.8 = 3.2 cm²"*. That is a typographical slip: 40 − 1.8 = **38.2**, not 3.2. The keyed letter matches the correct value, so only the printed working is wrong.

**Why the net section matters.** A tension member fails at its **weakest cross-section**, and bolt holes remove material precisely where the load must pass. IS 800 requires three checks on a tension member, and the net area governs the first:

| Failure mode | Design strength |
|---|---|
| **Net section rupture** | T_dn = **0.9 A_n f_u / γ_m1**, with γ_m1 = 1.25 |
| Gross section yielding | T_dg = A_g f_y / γ_m0, with γ_m0 = 1.10 |
| Block shear | T_db, from the shear and tension paths round the bolt group |

The member is designed for the **least** of the three. Note the different partial safety factors: rupture is a **brittle** failure at the ultimate strength, so it carries the larger factor (1.25), whereas gross yielding is ductile (1.10).

**Where the hole diameter comes from.** It is the **bolt diameter plus a clearance** — 1 mm for bolts up to 14 mm, **2 mm** for 16 to 24 mm, and 3 mm above that. So an 18 mm hole corresponds to a **16 mm bolt**. For a punched hole, an extra 2 mm is deducted, since punching damages the surrounding metal.

**With several bolts** the net area is taken along the **critical section**, and for staggered bolting the chain with the least net area governs:

> A_n = [b − n·d_h + Σ(p_s²/4g)] × t

where the p_s²/4g term credits back the extra material a staggered path must cross. Staggering bolts is done precisely to raise the net area, and the minimum pitch of **2.5 d** (Set 1 Q93) exists to keep the holes far enough apart for that to work.

verification.notes: The source's arithmetic line reads '40 − 1.8 = 3.2 cm²', a typographical slip for 38.2. The keyed option (a) is 38.2 cm² and is correct; only the printed working is in error.

examTip.trick: **Net area = (gross width − hole diameter) × thickness.** Remember the **hole is 1.5–2 mm larger than the bolt**, so a 20 mm bolt needs a 22 mm hole.
examTip.mnemonic: **Always deduct the HOLE, not the bolt.** For **staggered** holes add back **s²/4g** per stagger (the chain rule), and check every possible failure path — the critical chain is not always the obvious straight line across.

questions.stem: The simply supported beam 'A' of length l carries a central point load W. Another beam 'B' is loaded with a uniformly distributed load such that the total load on the beam is W. The ratio of maximum deflections between beams A and B is:
questions.solution:
**Option (b)** — the ratio is **8/5 = 1.6**.

**The two deflections**, both expressed in terms of the **total** load W as the question specifies:

> Beam A, central point load: δ_A = **WL³/(48EI)**
> Beam B, UDL of total load W: δ_B = **5WL³/(384EI)**

**The ratio:**
> δ_A/δ_B = [WL³/48EI] ÷ [5WL³/384EI]
> = 384/(48 × 5) = 384/240 = **1.6 = 8/5** ✓

So a **central point load deflects a beam 1.6 times as much** as the same total load spread uniformly — which makes physical sense, since the UDL places much of its weight near the supports where it does little bending.

**A note on the printed options.** All four carry an **L**, but the ratio of two deflections is **dimensionless** — L cannot appear in it. The spurious L arises from the source's working, which used the **total load W** for beam A but the load **intensity w** for beam B (δ = 5wL⁴/384EI). Mixing a total load with an intensity leaves one stray power of L, giving 8/(5L). Since the question explicitly states that the *total* load on beam B is also W, the correct ratio is **8/5**, and option (b) is the intended answer with the L disregarded.

That consistency check — **is the answer dimensionally possible?** — is worth applying routinely; here it identifies the source's error immediately.

**The standard deflection results**, worth holding as one table since the denominators are what get confused (all in terms of **total** load W):

| Beam and loading | Maximum deflection |
|---|---|
| **Simply supported, central point load** | **WL³/48EI** |
| **Simply supported, UDL** | **5WL³/384EI** |
| Fixed both ends, central point load | WL³/192EI |
| Fixed both ends, UDL | WL³/384EI |
| Cantilever, point load at end | WL³/3EI |
| Cantilever, UDL | WL³/8EI |

Two ratios worth noticing in that table. Comparing the simply supported and fixed cases under UDL gives **5:1** — fixing the ends reduces the deflection to one fifth, which is the structural value of continuity. And a cantilever under an end load deflects **16 times** as much as a simply supported beam of the same span under the same central load, which is why cantilevers are kept short and deep.

verification.notes: The ratio of two deflections is dimensionless, but all four printed options include an L. The stray L comes from the source's working, which used total load W for beam A and load intensity w for beam B. With both beams carrying total load W, as the stem states, the ratio is 8/5 — option (b) with the L disregarded.

examTip.trick: **δ ∝ L³/I** for a central point load. Compare the two beams by forming the ratio of L³/I and solving for the length that gives equal deflection.
examTip.mnemonic: **Deflection: L³ for a point load, L⁴ for a UDL, and I ∝ d³ for a rectangle.** Those three powers between them explain most of beam design — and why **depth** is always the most effective variable to change.

questions.stem: What is the ratio of the velocity at the axis of the pipe to the mean velocity of flow in case of pipe flow under viscous condition?
questions.solution:
**2.**

For **laminar (viscous)** flow in a circular pipe, the velocity profile is **parabolic**:

> u(r) = (Δp/4μL)(R² − r²)

**At the axis** (r = 0):
> u_max = ΔpR²/(4μL)

**The mean velocity** is obtained by integrating the profile over the cross-section:
> V = Q/A = ΔpR²/(8μL)

**The ratio:**
> **u_max/V = 8/4 = 2** ✓

So in laminar pipe flow the **centreline velocity is exactly twice the mean velocity** — a clean, exact result, arising purely from the geometry of a paraboloid: the mean ordinate of a parabola of revolution is half its peak.

**The contrast with turbulent flow** is worth holding alongside it:

| Regime | Profile | u_max/V |
|---|---|---|
| **Laminar** (Re < 2000) | **Parabolic** | **2.0** (exactly) |
| **Turbulent** (Re > 4000) | **Much flatter** — logarithmic or power law | ≈ **1.15 – 1.25** |

Turbulent mixing transports momentum across the section, flattening the profile so that most of the flow moves at nearly the same speed, with the velocity gradient confined to a thin layer at the wall. That is why the ratio drops towards 1.

**The practical use of the result.** A **pitot tube** on the pipe axis measures u_max directly. Dividing by the appropriate ratio gives the mean velocity, and hence the discharge Q = AV — which is how a single-point measurement is converted into a flow rate. Getting the regime wrong would introduce an error of nearly 100%.

The companion laminar-flow results, which come from the same profile:

> **Hagen–Poiseuille:** Q = πΔpD⁴/(128μL)
> **Head loss:** h_f = 32μVL/(γD²), so **h_f ∝ V** — the first power, not V²
> **Friction factor:** f = 64/Re (or coefficient of friction 16/Re, per Set 3 Q32)
> **Shear stress:** τ = (Δp/2L)·r — **linear**, zero at the axis and maximum at the wall

That last item is the classic pairing to keep straight, and Set 2 Q52 tests it directly: in laminar pipe flow the **velocity is parabolic with its maximum at the centre**, while the **shear stress is linear with zero at the centre**. Confusing the two is the commonest error in this topic.

examTip.trick: **Laminar** flow has a **parabolic** profile, and integrating it gives **V_mean = V_max/2** exactly — so the ratio V_max/V_mean is **2**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Laminar 2.0; TURBULENT about 1.22** (V_mean ≈ 0.82 V_max), because turbulent mixing flattens the profile. Using the wrong factor to convert a centreline Pitot reading into a discharge gives a **64% error** — so identify the regime first.

questions.stem: The magnetic bearing of a line is 32° and the magnetic declination is 10° 15' W. The true bearing is:
questions.solution:
**21° 45'.**

**The rule**, which depends on the direction of declination:

> **Declination East:** True bearing = Magnetic bearing **+** declination
> **Declination West:** True bearing = Magnetic bearing **−** declination

**Substituting**, with a **westerly** declination:
> True bearing = 32° 00' − 10° 15'
> = 31° 60' − 10° 15'
> = **21° 45'** ✓

Note that the answer is a **bearing**, so it carries no compass letter — options (c) and (d) wrongly append a W, which belongs to the *declination*, not to the resulting bearing.

**Why the sign works that way.** Magnetic declination is the angle between **true (geographic) north** and **magnetic north**. With a **west** declination the magnetic needle points west of true north, so every magnetic bearing is measured from a datum rotated anticlockwise — and the reading is therefore **larger** than the true bearing by the amount of the declination. Subtracting corrects it.

A memory aid: **"West is least, East is best"** — a westerly declination is subtracted, an easterly added.

**Why the correction matters.** Magnetic north is not fixed. Declination varies with **place** and with **time**, through:

| Variation | Character |
|---|---|
| **Secular** | Slow drift over decades — the largest effect; old surveys need recomputation |
| Annual | Small yearly cycle |
| Diurnal | Daily swing of a few minutes of arc |
| **Irregular** | Magnetic storms — can reach a degree or more |

Because of this, a **magnetic** bearing is only meaningful with its date and place; a **true** bearing is permanent. That is why survey records, land boundaries and legal descriptions are reduced to true bearings, and why an old plan quoting magnetic bearings must be corrected for the declination change since it was made.

**Local attraction** is a separate hazard: iron, steel structures, railway lines and power cables deflect the needle locally. It is detected by checking that the **fore and back bearings of a line differ by exactly 180°** — if they do not, one or both stations is affected, and the correction is carried forward from an unaffected line.

The related conversions, for completeness: **whole circle bearing** (0° to 360°) versus **reduced bearing** (quadrantal, 0° to 90° with a quadrant letter such as N21°45'E), and fore bearing versus back bearing differing by 180°.

examTip.trick: **True bearing = magnetic bearing + declination**, with an **easterly** declination taken as **positive** and a **westerly** one as **negative**. Here: 32° − 10°15′ = **21°45′**.
examTip.mnemonic: **"Variation EAST, magnetic LEAST; variation WEST, magnetic BEST."** An easterly declination is therefore **added** to the magnetic bearing and a westerly one **subtracted**. Getting the sign backwards is the whole trap, and the two answers differ by exactly twice the declination.

questions.stem: Negative skin friction on a pile:
options: Increases the load carrying capacity of the pile
Acts as an additional downward load on the pile
Has no effect on pile design
questions.solution:
**It acts as an additional downward load on the pile.**

Normally the soil supports the pile: as the pile tends to settle, friction along its shaft acts **upward** and contributes to the capacity. **Negative skin friction (downdrag)** is the reverse case — the **soil settles more than the pile**, so the friction reverses direction and drags the pile **down**.

The consequence is severe: instead of contributing capacity, that length of shaft becomes a **load**. The design capacity must be reduced accordingly:

> **Q_allowable = (Q_end bearing + Q_positive friction)/FoS − Q_negative friction**

Note that the downdrag is subtracted **after** the factor of safety, because it is a load and not a resistance.

**When it occurs:**

| Cause | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **Fill placed** over a compressible layer | The fill consolidates the clay beneath, which settles around the pile |
| **Lowering of the water table** | Raises effective stress, consolidating the soil |
| **Consolidation of a soft clay** under any surcharge | Ongoing settlement drags the shaft |
| Pile driven **through** a soft layer to a firm stratum | The soft layer settles while the pile is held by the firm one |

That last row is the classic case, and it explains why the problem arises precisely where piles are most obviously needed — driving through soft ground to something competent below.

**How it is reduced in practice:**
- **Bitumen coating** on the shaft over the settling zone, so the soil slips past the pile instead of gripping it — the most effective measure.
- A **casing or sleeve** isolating the shaft from the settling layer.
- **Pre-loading** the ground so consolidation is largely complete before the piles are installed.
- Increasing the pile length or size to carry the extra load.

**The pile capacity relations** it modifies:

> Q_u = Q_p + Q_s = q_p A_p + Σ f_s A_s
> **End bearing in clay:** q_p = **9 c_u** (Set 1 Q88)
> **Shaft friction in clay:** f_s = α c_u

Downdrag is one of the situations in which a **pile load test** is especially valuable, since the theoretical estimate is sensitive to how much of the shaft is affected and for how long.

examTip.trap: "Increases the capacity" is the natural but exactly backwards reading — friction usually helps, so people assume all friction helps.
examTip.trick: Ask **which moves more**. Normally the **pile** settles relative to the soil, so friction acts **upward**. Where the **soil** settles more — consolidating fill, lowered water table, remoulded clay reconsolidating — the relationship reverses.
examTip.mnemonic: **Q_net = Q_ultimate − Q_negative: SUBTRACT it.** The remedy is a **bitumen slip coating over the settling layer only** — coating the bearing length would remove the useful friction too.

questions.stem: A differential manometer is used to measure:
options: Difference of pressure between two points
Velocity of flow at a point
questions.solution:
**The difference of pressure between two points.**

A **differential** manometer connects **two** points in a system and reads the pressure difference between them directly from the deflection of the manometric fluid — usually mercury, for a compact reading:

> **p₁ − p₂ = h(γ_m − γ_f)**

where h is the manometer deflection, γ_m the specific weight of the manometric fluid and γ_f that of the flowing fluid.

The pressure-measuring devices, distinguished by what each reads:

| Device | Measures |
|---|---|
| **Piezometer** | **Gauge pressure at one point** — a simple open tube |
| Simple U-tube manometer | Gauge pressure at one point, including vacuum |
| **Differential manometer** | **Pressure difference between two points** |
| Inverted differential manometer | Small pressure differences (lighter fluid above) |
| Micromanometer | Very small differences, with magnification |
| **Barometer** | **Atmospheric pressure** |
| Bourdon gauge | Gauge pressure, mechanically |

So option (a) belongs to a **barometer**, and (b) requires adding atmospheric pressure to a gauge reading, since p_abs = p_atm + p_gauge.

**Why the pressure difference is the quantity wanted.** Almost every flow measurement is really a pressure-difference measurement, because Bernoulli converts a pressure drop into a velocity:

| Application | What the Δp gives |
|---|---|
| **Venturimeter, orifice meter, nozzle meter** | **Discharge**, Q = C_d A₁A₂√(2gh)/√(A₁²−A₂²) |
| **Pitot tube** | **Velocity**, v = C_v√(2gh) |
| Along a pipe run | **Friction head loss** h_f, hence the friction factor |

So option (d) is not wrong in spirit — a differential manometer is exactly what one uses to *find* a velocity — but it measures the **pressure difference** from which velocity is then computed.

**Practical points.** The manometric fluid must be **denser and immiscible** with the flowing fluid; mercury (relative density 13.6) gives small, readable deflections for large pressure differences, while for small differences a lighter fluid or an **inclined tube** magnifies the reading. And the tube bore should exceed about **6 mm** so that capillary error can be neglected — the 1/d law of Q64 of this paper.

examTip.trick: A **simple** manometer measures pressure **at one point** against atmosphere; a **differential** manometer connects **two points** and reads the difference directly.
examTip.mnemonic: **h = x(S_m/S_f − 1) — and the −1 is the term everyone forgets.** For mercury under water that is **× 12.6, not × 13.6**. The rising mercury displaces the water that was there, so the net effect is the *difference* in weights.

questions.stem: In the rational method of estimating peak run-off, the runoff coefficient C represents the ratio of:
options: Peak run-off rate to rainfall intensity
Total run-off volume to catchment area
questions.solution:
**The ratio of peak run-off rate to rainfall intensity** — that is, the fraction of the rainfall that appears as run-off.

**The rational formula:**
> **Q = C · I · A** (in consistent units)
> Q = **0.278 C I A** with Q in m³/s, I in mm/h and A in km²

So **C is dimensionless**, and it expresses how much of the rain runs off rather than infiltrating, evaporating or being intercepted. A dimensional check disposes of the wrong options immediately: (a) and (c) would carry units, and (d) describes the *complement* of C.

Typical values, which show how strongly land use dominates:

| Surface | C |
|---|---|
| **Bituminous or concrete pavement, roofs** | **0.70 – 0.95** |
| Bare compacted soil | 0.50 – 0.70 |
| Gravel roads | 0.35 – 0.70 |
| Lawns and parks, sandy soil | **0.05 – 0.20** |
| Cultivated land | 0.20 – 0.40 |
| Forested land | 0.10 – 0.30 |

Hence **urbanisation raises C dramatically** — the same storm on a paved catchment produces several times the peak flow it would from open ground. That is the single most important fact in urban drainage, and the reason Kathmandu's flooding has worsened as the valley has been built over.

For a mixed catchment, a **weighted** value is used: C = Σ(C_i A_i)/ΣA.

**The other essential idea — the time of concentration t_c.** The rational method assumes rainfall lasting at least as long as t_c, the time for run-off to travel from the remotest point of the catchment to the outlet. Only then does the whole area contribute simultaneously, giving the peak. So the design intensity I is read from the **intensity–duration–frequency curve at a duration equal to t_c**, for the chosen return period. Since IDF curves fall steeply with duration, a small catchment (short t_c) takes a much higher intensity than a large one.

**Assumptions and limits**, which is why the method is called *rational* rather than exact:
- Rainfall uniform over the catchment and constant for the duration.
- C constant, taking no account of antecedent wetness or of storage.
- Return period of the run-off equal to that of the rainfall.

These hold reasonably for **small catchments — up to about 50 km²**, and the method is standard for **storm sewers, road culverts and side drains**. For larger catchments, unit hydrograph methods (Set 2 Q87) or the regional formulae of Set 2 Q17 are used instead.

examTip.trick: **Q = CIA**, so **C = Q/(IA)** — the runoff coefficient is the fraction of the rainfall that becomes runoff, once the areas and units are consistent.
examTip.mnemonic: **C: paved 0.7–0.95, lawns 0.05–0.20, cultivated 0.20–0.40.** Two constant traps in this method: the intensity must be read at a duration equal to the **TIME OF CONCENTRATION**, and the method is valid only for **small catchments** (under about 25–50 km²).

questions.stem: Rankine's formula for the crippling load of a column is applicable to:
questions.solution:
**Both short and long columns.**

Rankine's formula was devised precisely because **Euler's formula fails for short columns**. Euler gives

> P_cr = π²EI/l_e²

which tends to **infinity** as the length tends to zero — plainly absurd, since a very short column simply crushes at its compressive strength.

**Rankine's empirical formula** bridges the two behaviours:

> **P = σ_c · A / [1 + a(l_e/k)²]**

where σ_c is the crushing stress, k the least radius of gyration, and a = σ_c/(π²E) is Rankine's constant (1/7500 for mild steel, 1/1600 for cast iron, 1/750 for timber).

**Why it works at both ends of the range** — examine the denominator:

| Column | Slenderness l_e/k | Denominator | Formula reduces to |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Short** | Small | ≈ 1 | **P ≈ σ_c A — pure crushing** |
| **Long** | Large | Dominated by a(l_e/k)² | **P ≈ π²EI/l_e² — Euler buckling** |
| Intermediate | Moderate | Both terms matter | A smooth blend of the two |

So a single expression covers the whole range and is exact at neither extreme but reasonable throughout — which is exactly what a design formula needs to be. It is derived by combining the two reciprocals:

> 1/P = 1/P_crushing + 1/P_Euler

**The failure modes it spans:**

| Column | Slenderness (steel) | Failure |
|---|---|---|
| Short | l_e/k < ~32 | **Crushing** |
| Intermediate | 32 – 120 | Combined — **Rankine's range** |
| Long | > 120 | **Buckling** |

Euler's formula additionally assumes an **ideal** column — perfectly straight, homogeneous, axially loaded — none of which is true in practice. Rankine's constant absorbs those imperfections empirically, which is another reason it is the more useful of the two for real members.

Option (d) is wrong on its face: the formula uses the **radius of gyration**, so it applies to any section whose k can be computed — and note that k must be the **least** value, since buckling occurs about the weak axis (Q53 of this paper).

Modern codes have moved beyond both: IS 800 uses **multiple column curves** based on the Perry–Robertson approach, with buckling class depending on the section shape and the axis considered, so that residual stresses and initial curvature are treated explicitly.

examTip.trick: **Rankine's formula P = f_c A/(1 + a(L_e/k)²)** is designed to cover the whole range: at **small slenderness** it tends to the crushing load f_c A, and at **large slenderness** it approaches the Euler load.
examTip.mnemonic: **Euler is valid for LONG columns only** (above the critical slenderness, about 80 for mild steel) — below that it gives absurdly high loads. **Rankine bridges both**, which is exactly why it survives despite being empirical.

questions.stem: In the method of joints for analysing a truss, the analysis must begin at a joint where the number of unknown member forces does not exceed:
questions.solution:
**Two.**

At each joint of a **plane** truss, all the member forces are **concurrent** — they pass through a single point — so no moment equation is available. Only two independent equilibrium equations remain:

> **ΣF_x = 0** and **ΣF_y = 0**

Two equations can solve at most **two unknowns**. So the analysis must start at a joint with no more than two unknown member forces, solve them, and then move to an adjacent joint where the newly found forces reduce the unknown count to two again.

That is the whole procedure:
1. Find the **support reactions** from overall equilibrium of the truss.
2. Identify a joint with **≤ 2 unknowns** — typically a support joint, or the free end of the truss.
3. Apply ΣF_x = 0 and ΣF_y = 0 to find them.
4. Progress joint by joint, each time choosing one with only two remaining unknowns.

**Sign convention and its usefulness:** assume every member is in **tension** (force pulling away from the joint). A **negative** answer then means the member is in **compression**, with no need to guess in advance.

**When the method of joints is the wrong tool.** If the force in only one or two particular members is wanted — especially in a long truss where those members are far from the ends — working joint by joint from the support is wasteful. The **method of sections** is then used instead: cut through the truss (through at most **three** members) and apply **three** equations, ΣF_x, ΣF_y and **ΣM**, to the free body. Taking moments about a suitable point isolates one unknown directly.

| | **Method of joints** | **Method of sections** |
|---|---|---|
| Equations per step | **2** (ΣF_x, ΣF_y) | **3** (ΣF_x, ΣF_y, **ΣM**) |
| Unknowns solvable | **2** | **3** |
| Suits | **All** member forces | A **few specific** members |

**Zero-force members** are worth spotting first, since they shorten the work considerably:
- At an **unloaded two-member joint** with the members non-collinear, **both** carry zero force.
- At an **unloaded three-member joint** where two members are collinear, the **third** carries zero force.

The method assumes what all truss analysis assumes: **pin joints, loads applied only at joints, and straight members**, so every member carries pure axial force with no bending. Real trusses have bolted or welded joints that transmit some moment, but the resulting **secondary stresses** are small and normally neglected — provided loads are indeed brought to the joints, which is why purlins are placed at panel points.

examTip.trick: Each joint gives only **two** equations (ΣH = 0 and ΣV = 0), so a joint with more than two unknown member forces cannot be solved on its own.
examTip.mnemonic: **Method of JOINTS: start where only TWO unknowns meet, then work outward. Method of SECTIONS: cut through at most THREE unknown members** (three equations available: ΣH, ΣV, ΣM). Use sections when you want one specific member force without solving the whole truss.

questions.stem: In seismic design, the response reduction factor R accounts for:
options: The ductility and energy absorption capacity of the structure
The soil type at the site
questions.solution:
**The ductility and energy absorption capacity of the structure.**

The design horizontal seismic coefficient is

> **A_h = (Z/2) · (I/R) · (S_a/g)**

and each factor accounts for a distinct thing — which is exactly what this question tests:

| Factor | Accounts for |
|---|---|
| **Z** — zone factor | **Seismic hazard** of the region |
| **I** — importance factor | **Consequence of failure** — hospitals, schools, lifeline structures |
| **S_a/g** — spectral acceleration | **Structural period** and the **soil type** at the site |
| **R** — response reduction factor | **Ductility and energy absorption** — the structure's ability to deform inelastically without collapsing |

So options (c) and (d) belong to S_a/g and I respectively, and mass enters separately through the seismic weight W in V_B = A_h W.

**What R actually represents.** A structure is *not* designed to remain elastic in the design earthquake — that would be prohibitively expensive. It is designed to be **damaged but not collapse**, dissipating energy through controlled inelastic deformation at chosen locations. R is the factor by which the elastic force demand may be divided in recognition of that capacity.

> **A more ductile system earns a higher R, and therefore a lower design force.**

Typical values from IS 1893:

| Structural system | R |
|---|---|
| Ordinary RC moment resisting frame (OMRF) | **3.0** |
| **Special RC moment resisting frame (SMRF)** | **5.0** |
| Steel frame with concentric bracing | 4.0 |
| **Unreinforced masonry** | **1.5** |

The contrast between the last two rows is the practical lesson: an SMRF may be designed for a force **more than three times smaller** than unreinforced masonry — but only because it is **detailed** to deliver that ductility.

**The obligation R imposes.** Claiming a high R is a promise about detailing, and the promise must be kept through the provisions of IS 13920 / NBC 105:
- **Closely spaced closed stirrups** with 135° hooks in the confining zones at member ends;
- **Strong column–weak beam** proportioning, so hinges form in beams (repairable, and non-collapsing) rather than in columns;
- **Capacity design for shear** — shear capacity exceeding the shear corresponding to flexural hinging, so the brittle mode never governs;
- Adequate **development length and continuity** of reinforcement through joints.

Use SMRF values without SMRF detailing and the structure is under-designed by a factor of nearly two — a failure mode observed repeatedly in the **2015 Gorkha earthquake**, alongside the **soft storey** problem created by open ground floors.

The companion combination rule from Set 2 Q61: directional effects are combined as **100% in one direction with 30% in the orthogonal direction**.

examTip.trick: **R** divides the elastic design force down to a level a **ductile** structure can survive by yielding. A structure with more ductility and better detailing gets a **higher R** and hence a **smaller design force**.
examTip.mnemonic: **A higher R means a SMALLER design force — but it is EARNED by detailing.** Claiming a ductile R and then detailing the structure ordinarily is one of the most dangerous errors in seismic design, because the whole design assumed a plastic capacity that was never built in. That is what **IS 13920 / NBC 105** ductile detailing provides.
