questions.stem: As per IS 456, the pitch of lateral ties in an RC column shall not exceed:
options: The least lateral dimension of the column
questions.solution:
**The least lateral dimension of the column** — this being the first of three limits, all of which must be satisfied.

IS 456 cl. 26.5.3.2 requires the pitch of lateral ties to be the **least** of:

| Limit | Value |
|---|---|
| 1 | **The least lateral dimension** of the column |
| 2 | **16 × the smallest diameter** of the longitudinal reinforcement |
| 3 | **300 mm** |

and the **tie diameter** must be at least the greater of **¼ of the largest longitudinal bar** or **6 mm**.

**Worked example** — a 300 × 400 mm column with 20 mm main bars:
> Least lateral dimension = 300 mm
> 16 × 20 = 320 mm
> Absolute limit = 300 mm
> **Pitch = 300 mm**, tie diameter ≥ max(20/4, 6) = **6 mm**

**What the ties are actually for.** They are not there to carry load in the ordinary sense, but to:

- **Prevent buckling of the longitudinal bars** between tie levels. A slender bar in compression will buckle outward, spalling the cover; the ties provide lateral restraint at intervals. This is why the 16φ limit is tied to the *bar* diameter.
- **Confine the concrete core**, so that under high compression it is restrained laterally and can sustain much greater axial strain before failing.
- **Resist shear**, and hold the reinforcement cage in position during concreting.

The confinement function is decisive in **seismic** design. Confined concrete is far more **ductile** than unconfined concrete: it continues to carry load at large strains rather than crushing and spalling suddenly. That is why IS 13920 tightens the requirements greatly in the **confining zones** at the member ends:

| | Ordinary (IS 456) | Ductile detailing (IS 13920) |
|---|---|---|
| Spacing in confining zone | Up to 300 mm | **≤ 100 mm** typically |
| Hook angle | 90° acceptable | **135° hooks**, embedded into the core |
| Tie form | Simple rectangular | **Closed hoops**, with cross-ties |

The **135° hook** matters more than it appears: a 90° hook opens out and the tie unravels once the cover spalls, precisely when confinement is most needed. This detail was a repeated cause of column failure in the 2015 Gorkha earthquake.

The related longitudinal-steel limits for columns: **minimum 0.8%** and **maximum 6%** of the gross area (4% preferred for practical placing), with a **minimum of 4 bars** in a rectangular column and **6 bars** in a circular one. And note from Set 1 Q24 that a **helically reinforced** circular column earns a 1.05 strength multiplier under IS 456 cl. 39.4 — a direct reward for the better confinement a continuous spiral provides.

examTip.trick: The **pitch of lateral ties** is the least of: **the least lateral dimension of the column**, **16 × the smallest longitudinal bar diameter**, and **300 mm**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Least dimension, 16φ, or 300 mm — take the smallest.** Ties do three jobs: hold the bars in position, prevent the longitudinal bars **BUCKLING** outward, and **CONFINE** the core concrete. In a seismic zone the spacing is tightened drastically in the plastic hinge zones — which is where confinement earns its ductility.

questions.stem: As per IS 1172, the domestic water demand per capita per day for a town with full flushing system is taken as:
questions.solution:
**135 litres per capita per day.**

IS 1172 breaks the domestic allowance down by use, and the total is worth knowing item by item because the examination asks for the components as often as the sum:

| Use | Litres per capita per day |
|---|---|
| **Flushing of WC** | **45** |
| Bathing | 55 |
| Washing of clothes | 20 |
| Washing of utensils | 10 |
| Cooking | 5 |
| **Drinking** | **5** |
| **Total domestic** | **135** |

Note that **flushing alone accounts for a third** of the total — which is why low-flush and dual-flush cisterns make a real difference to demand, and why the figure is quoted as applying to a *full flushing system*.

**The total demand for a town** is much larger than the domestic figure, and the two are frequently confused:

| Component | lpcd |
|---|---|
| **Domestic** | **135** |
| Industrial and commercial | 70 |
| Public and institutional | 25 |
| Losses, waste and theft | 55 |
| **Total** | **≈ 270 – 335** |

So option (d), 270 lpcd, is the **total** per capita demand for an Indian city — the standard distractor here.

**Nepali practice** uses lower figures, reflecting service levels: about **45 to 65 lpcd for rural** schemes and **100 to 135 lpcd for urban** areas, per the Department of Water Supply and Sewerage design guidelines.

**How the design demands are built up from the average**, which is the reason per capita demand matters at all:

| Demand | Multiplier on average daily | Governs |
|---|---|---|
| Average daily | 1.0 | Source capacity, treatment plant |
| **Maximum daily** | **1.8** | Pumps, treatment, transmission main |
| **Maximum hourly (peak)** | **2.7** (i.e. 1.5 × max daily) | **Distribution mains, service reservoir** |
| Coincident draft | Max daily **+ fire demand** | Mains near hydrants |

So the distribution network is sized for roughly **2.7 times** the average — and the fire demand of Q70 of this paper is added on top where hydrants are served.

The **design period** for the works is chosen by component: 30 years or more for a dam or a large main, 15 years for a treatment plant, 10 years for pumps — since a pipe is expensive to replace but a pump is not. **Population forecasting** (arithmetic, geometric, incremental increase or logistic methods) then converts today's per capita figure into tomorrow's total demand.

examTip.trick: **135 litres per capita per day** for a town with full flushing systems, broken into domestic uses: bathing 55, flushing 30, washing clothes 20, cooking 5, drinking 5, utensils 10.
examTip.mnemonic: **135 lpcd domestic; total demand adds industrial, commercial, public and fire, plus losses.** Then apply the peak factors: **maximum daily 1.8 × average, maximum hourly 1.5 × maximum daily**, so the peak hour is about **2.7 × average** — which is what sizes the distribution mains.

questions.stem: In the design of a sedimentation tank, the surface overflow rate is defined as:
options: Discharge per unit surface area of the tank
Discharge per unit volume of the tank
Detention time divided by the depth
Velocity of flow along the tank
questions.solution:
**Discharge per unit surface area** of the tank:

> **Surface overflow rate = Q/A_surface** (m³/m²/day, equivalently m/day)

It has the units of a **velocity**, and that is exactly what it physically is — the **critical settling velocity**. A particle whose settling velocity exceeds the overflow rate will reach the floor before the flow carries it out; one that settles more slowly escapes with the effluent.

> **v_settling ≥ Q/A** → particle removed

**The consequence that makes this the central idea of sedimentation design.** Removal efficiency depends on the tank's **surface area, not its volume or its depth**. Two tanks of the same plan area remove the same particles even if one is twice as deep — the deeper tank merely holds the water longer without improving separation. That is why:

- Sedimentation tanks are designed **shallow and wide** rather than deep;
- **Tube settlers and plate settlers** work: by inserting inclined plates they multiply the effective settling area within the same tank volume, greatly increasing capacity;
- Increasing detention time alone does **not** improve removal, though it is still specified to ensure adequate hydraulic performance.

**Typical design values:**

| Parameter | Plain sedimentation | After coagulation (clariflocculator) |
|---|---|---|
| **Surface overflow rate** | **20 – 30 m³/m²/day** | 30 – 40 m³/m²/day |
| **Detention time** | **3 – 4 hours** | 2 – 2.5 hours |
| Horizontal velocity | 0.3 – 1.0 cm/s | — |
| Weir loading | 100 – 300 m³/m/day | — |
| Depth | 3 – 4.5 m | 3 – 4.5 m |

Option (d), the horizontal velocity along the tank, is a **different** quantity — Q divided by the *cross-sectional* area — and it is limited separately to prevent scouring of already-settled sludge.

**The underlying physics** is **Stokes' law**, which governs the settling of discrete particles in the laminar range:

> v_s = g(G_s − 1)d²/(18ν)

The **d²** dependence is decisive: halving the particle size **quarters** the settling velocity. Colloidal clay particles, at around 0.001 mm, would take months to settle — which is precisely why **coagulation with alum** is needed to agglomerate them into flocs large enough to settle in hours (Set 2 Q55).

Where sedimentation sits in the treatment train: **screening → aeration → coagulation and flocculation → sedimentation → filtration → disinfection**. Sedimentation removes the bulk of the suspended load so that the filters are not overwhelmed; a filter is a polishing step, not a substitute for settling.

examTip.trick: **Surface loading rate (overflow rate) = Q/A_surface**, and it has the units of a **velocity** — m³/m²/day, which is m/day.
examTip.mnemonic: **A particle settles out if its settling velocity EXCEEDS the overflow rate** — which means removal depends on the tank's **SURFACE AREA, not its depth**. That is the single counter-intuitive result of sedimentation theory, and it is why tanks are made shallow and wide rather than deep.

questions.stem: The most environmentally acceptable method of disposing of municipal solid waste in a controlled manner is:
questions.solution:
**Sanitary landfilling.**

A sanitary landfill is an **engineered** facility — quite unlike the open dump it is routinely confused with. Waste is placed in prepared cells, compacted, and covered with earth daily, and the site is designed from the outset to contain its own pollution:

| Component | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **Impermeable liner** (clay and/or geomembrane) | Prevents **leachate** reaching groundwater |
| **Leachate collection and treatment** | Intercepts and treats the contaminated liquid draining from the waste |
| **Gas venting or recovery** | Landfill gas is roughly 50% **methane** — explosive, and a potent greenhouse gas; it can be flared or used for energy |
| **Daily earth cover** | Controls odour, flies, rodents, litter and fire |
| Final capping and restoration | Sheds rainwater, permits after-use of the land |
| Monitoring wells | Confirm that groundwater is not being contaminated |

Why the alternatives are unacceptable: **open dumping** (a) contaminates groundwater with uncontrolled leachate and breeds disease vectors; **river discharge** (c) is straightforwardly illegal and destroys the water source; **open burning** (b) releases dioxins and particulates and is prohibited.

**Where landfilling sits in the hierarchy**, which is the more important point. Landfill is the **last** resort, not the first:

> **Reduce → Reuse → Recycle → Recover (compost, energy) → Dispose (landfill)**

Since the organic fraction of Nepali municipal waste is high — **60 to 70%** — **composting** is particularly appropriate, and it both diverts the bulk of the waste stream and produces a saleable soil conditioner. Waste-to-energy incineration is generally unsuited to waste of such high moisture and low calorific value.

**The two decomposition regimes** matter for design:

| Phase | Duration | Products |
|---|---|---|
| **Aerobic** | Days to weeks | CO₂, water, heat |
| **Anaerobic** | **Years to decades** | **Methane**, CO₂, organic acids; strong leachate |

The long anaerobic phase is why a closed landfill needs **post-closure care and monitoring for decades**, and why gas management is not optional.

In Nepal these requirements fall under the **Solid Waste Management Act 2068**, which places the duty on local bodies, and the **Environment Protection Act 2076**, under which a landfill requires an **EIA**. The practical difficulty is the familiar one: siting. A landfill needs impermeable ground, a deep water table, distance from settlement and surface water, and secure road access — and it invariably meets local opposition, which is why Kathmandu's disposal arrangements have remained unresolved for so long.

examTip.trick: Rank disposal methods by environmental control: **open dumping** (worst — uncontrolled leachate and gas), **open burning** (air pollution), **incineration** (needs control and produces ash), **sanitary landfill** (engineered liner, leachate collection, gas capture, daily cover).
examTip.mnemonic: **A SANITARY landfill is engineered; a DUMP is not — the difference is the liner, the leachate collection and the daily cover.** Above it in the waste hierarchy sit **reduce, reuse, recycle and compost**; landfill is the last resort, not the first choice.

questions.stem: The base period of a crop is:
options: Always equal to the crop period
Slightly more than the crop period
questions.solution:
**Slightly more than the crop period.**

The two periods differ at both ends, and the distinction is precise:

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Crop period** | From **sowing to harvesting** — the life of the crop in the field |
| **Base period** | From the **first watering** (which precedes sowing, for land preparation) to the **last watering** before harvest |

Because the first watering is applied **before** sowing, the base period begins earlier than the crop period, and it therefore comes out **slightly longer**. The two are close enough that they are often taken as equal in rough calculations — but they are not identical, and the base period is the correct one for design.

**Why the base period is what enters the formulae.** Irrigation supply is required over the whole watering season, not merely the growing season, so the base period is the B in

> **Δ = 8.64 B / D**

where Δ is the delta in metres, B the base period in **days** and D the duty in **hectares per cumec**. The constant 8.64 = 86,400 s per day ÷ 10,000 m² per hectare carries the unit conversion.

Typical values:

| Crop | Base period (days) | Delta (cm) |
|---|---|---|
| **Rice** | **120** | **100 – 125** |
| Wheat | 120 | 40 |
| Sugarcane | **360** | 90 – 100 |
| Cotton | 200 | 50 |
| Maize | 100 | 25 |

Note the **inverse relationship** between duty and delta: a crop with a large delta (rice) has a correspondingly low duty, because one cumec then irrigates less land.

**Where the kor requirement fits.** Within the base period there is a short critical spell soon after sowing — the **kor period** — when the crop needs its first and most important watering, of depth equal to the **kor depth**. Because this is the peak demand of the season, the **capacity of the outlet and distributary is fixed by the kor requirement**, not by the seasonal average. That is why the duty computed from kor figures is called the **outlet factor** (Set 3 Q65: kor depth 190 mm over 14 days gives 637 ha/cumec for rice).

The two cropping seasons in Nepal and northern India, examined alongside: **Kharif** (monsoon — rice, maize, cotton, sown June–July) and **Rabi** (winter — wheat, barley, mustard, sown October–November), with **Zaid** the short hot-weather season between them. The **intensity of irrigation** is the percentage of the culturable command area actually irrigated in a season, and the sum over both seasons can exceed 100% where land is double-cropped.

examTip.trick: **Crop period** is from sowing to harvest; **base period** is from the **first watering to the last** — which extends slightly beyond, because the first watering precedes sowing and the last precedes harvest.
examTip.mnemonic: **Base period is slightly MORE than the crop period, and the two are often taken as equal in problems.** It matters because **Δ = 8.64B/D** uses the base period B — using the crop period instead gives a slightly low depth of water.

questions.stem: A canal fall is provided when:
options: The ground slope is steeper than the designed canal bed slope
The canal has to cross a natural drain
The canal discharge has to be measured
Surplus water has to be discharged out of the canal
questions.solution:
**When the ground slope is steeper than the designed canal bed slope.**

A canal must be laid to a **gentle, non-scouring** bed slope — typically 1 in 5,000 to 1 in 10,000, fixed by the regime or non-silting-non-scouring requirement. Natural ground often falls much more steeply than that. If the canal simply followed the ground it would run too fast and scour; if it kept its own gentle slope it would soon stand high above the ground on an uneconomically deep embankment.

The resolution is to keep the gentle slope over each reach and **drop the bed abruptly** at intervals in a controlled structure — a **canal fall** (or drop). The surplus elevation is surrendered at a point where the energy can be safely dissipated, instead of being converted into damaging velocity along the whole length.

> **Purpose: lower the canal bed level, and dissipate the surplus energy safely.**

Why the other options name different structures — this is the standard set, and each has one job:

| Situation | Structure |
|---|---|
| **Ground steeper than canal slope** | **Canal fall (drop)** |
| Canal crosses a natural drain | **Cross-drainage work** — aqueduct, syphon aqueduct, super passage, canal syphon (Set 3 Q47) |
| Discharge must be **measured** | **Metering flume**, standing wave flume, or a **flume-type fall** |
| **Surplus water** must be let out | **Canal escape** (Set 2 Q32) |
| Discharge into an offtake must be **controlled** | Canal regulator |
| Sanctioned share delivered to a field | Canal outlet / module |

**Types of fall**, in order of development:

| Type | Character |
|---|---|
| Ogee fall | Smooth ogee profile; little energy dissipated — early design |
| **Vertical drop (Sarda type)** | Nappe drops onto a cistern; simple and widely used |
| Glacis fall | Sloping glacis; hydraulic jump forms on it |
| **Baffle fall** | Baffle wall in the cistern to force and hold the jump — very effective |
| Well type / cylinder fall | For small canals with a large drop |
| **Flume fall** | Throat flumed so the fall **also meters** the discharge |

That last row is worth noting: a **flumed fall serves two purposes at once**, dropping the bed and measuring the flow, which is why falls are often deliberately combined with metering.

**The design essential is energy dissipation.** Water arrives at the toe of a fall as **supercritical** flow, and it must be returned to the subcritical regime of the downstream canal through a **hydraulic jump** contained within a cistern. The cistern is proportioned so that the jump forms and stays put — using the sequent-depth relation y₂/y₁ = ½(√(1+8Fr₁²) − 1) and a length of about 5 to 7 times the jump height (Set 1 Q34). If the jump sweeps out of the cistern, the high-velocity jet attacks the canal bed and scours it — the same failure logic as an under-designed spillway stilling basin.

examTip.trick: If the **ground falls faster than the canal needs to**, the canal would end up in deep cutting or the velocity would become erosive. A fall drops the bed in a controlled step and dissipates the surplus energy.
examTip.mnemonic: **Ground steeper than the canal → provide FALLS.** They are often combined with other functions: a **fall with a regulator**, or a **fall with a bridge or a hydropower installation** — since the drop is a free source of head.

questions.stem: In Nepal, the license for the survey, generation, transmission and distribution of electricity is issued by:
questions.solution:
**Department of Electricity Development (DoED).**

The institutions in Nepal's power sector have distinct and frequently confused roles, and licensing is the specific function of DoED:

| Institution | Role |
|---|---|
| **DoED** — Department of Electricity Development | **Licensing authority** — issues survey, generation, transmission and distribution licenses; promotes and regulates private sector development |
| **NEA** — Nepal Electricity Authority | The **state-owned utility** — generates, transmits and distributes power; the principal off-taker buying from independent producers |
| **WECS** — Water and Energy Commission Secretariat | **Policy, planning and studies**; the source of national hydropower potential estimates |
| **ERC** — Electricity Regulatory Commission | **Economic regulator** — tariffs, PPA review, consumer protection (established 2074/2017) |
| **NEC** — Nepal Engineering Council | Registers **engineers**; nothing to do with electricity licensing |

So option (a) names the **utility**, (c) the **professional regulator** for engineers, and (b) the **planning body** — none of them the licensing authority.

**The license sequence for a hydropower project**, which is what a candidate is really being asked to know:

1. **Survey license** — permits investigation and feasibility study, typically for up to 5 years.
2. **Generation license** — permits construction and operation, granted for up to **50 years**, after which the project transfers to the Government.
3. **Power Purchase Agreement (PPA)** with NEA, fixing the tariff and term.
4. **Environmental clearance** — IEE or **EIA** under the Environment Protection Act 2076, depending on capacity.

That 50-year term and reversion is essentially a **BOOT** arrangement (Set 3 Q73): the developer builds, owns and operates the plant, recovering its investment from the PPA, and ownership transfers to the State at the end.

**Why the framework exists.** Nepal's theoretical hydropower potential is about **83,000 MW**, of which roughly **42,000 MW** is considered technically and economically feasible, against a few thousand MW developed. Opening the sector to **independent power producers** under the Electricity Act 2049 (1992) was the policy response, and the licensing regime administered by DoED is the mechanism.

A note on capacity thresholds, since they affect which approvals are needed: very small schemes are exempt from licensing altogether, and the environmental study tier — **BES, IEE or EIA** — steps up with installed capacity, as does the level of government granting approval.

examTip.trick: In Nepal, the survey, generation, transmission and distribution license for electricity is issued by the **Department of Electricity Development** under the Ministry of Energy.
examTip.mnemonic: **Survey license first (typically 2–5 years), then the generation license (up to 35 years for hydropower), then the project reverts to the Government.** Keep the roles apart: the **DoED licenses**, the **NEA** has historically been the utility, and the **Electricity Regulatory Commission** regulates tariffs.

questions.stem: A two-part electricity tariff consists of:
options: A fixed charge based on maximum demand plus a running charge based on energy consumed
Two different rates for two categories of consumer
Two separate meters for lighting and power
A flat rate charged twice a year
questions.solution:
**A fixed charge based on maximum demand, plus a running charge based on energy consumed.**

> **Total charge = a × kW (maximum demand) + b × kWh (energy)**

The structure mirrors the supplier's own cost structure, which is why it is used:

| Component | Recovers | Depends on |
|---|---|---|
| **Fixed / demand charge** | **Capital cost** — generation capacity, transmission, distribution, interest, depreciation | The **peak demand** the system must be built to meet |
| **Running / energy charge** | **Operating cost** — fuel, water, maintenance, losses | The **energy** actually delivered |

The insight is that a consumer who draws a large peak imposes a capacity cost on the system **even if total consumption is modest**, because the plant and cables must be sized for that peak. A pure energy tariff would let such a consumer under-pay, with the cost falling on everyone else.

The main tariff forms:

| Tariff | Structure | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **Flat rate** | Rs/kWh only | Simple; ignores demand entirely |
| Block rate | Rate falls (or rises) in consumption blocks | Rising blocks used for **social pricing** — cheap lifeline units, dearer above |
| **Two-part** | **Demand charge + energy charge** | The standard commercial and industrial tariff |
| Three-part | Fixed + demand + energy | Adds a customer service charge |
| **Time-of-day (TOD)** | Rate varies by hour | Charges more at **peak**, less off-peak |
| Power factor tariff | Penalty / rebate on power factor | Encourages reactive power correction |

**Why this matters to the system, not merely to billing.** A two-part tariff gives the consumer a direct financial reason to **flatten their own load curve** — to avoid an unnecessary peak — and hence to raise the system **load factor**:

> Load factor = average demand / peak demand

A higher load factor means the same plant delivers more energy, so the capital cost is spread over more units and the cost per unit falls. Tariff design is therefore a demand-management tool as much as a revenue mechanism, and **time-of-day** tariffs extend the same logic to shifting consumption in time.

**In Nepal** this is particularly pointed. Tariffs are set by the **Electricity Regulatory Commission**, and the system's dominant problem is **seasonal**: run-of-river plants produce abundantly in the monsoon and little in winter (Set 2 Q94), so the peak-versus-off-peak distinction is compounded by a wet-versus-dry-season one. Industrial tariffs accordingly include demand charges and time-of-day elements, and dedicated feeders and off-peak rates are used to encourage consumption when generation is surplus.

examTip.trick: A two-part tariff separates the utility's two kinds of cost: **fixed costs** (capacity, which depends on the customer's maximum demand) and **variable costs** (fuel and energy actually consumed).
examTip.mnemonic: **Fixed charge on MAXIMUM DEMAND + running charge on ENERGY.** It is fairer because a customer with a spiky load forces the utility to build capacity it rarely uses — and it gives the customer a direct incentive to **improve their load factor** by flattening their demand.

questions.stem: The primary function of a trash rack at a hydropower intake is to:
options: Remove dissolved salts from the water
Dissipate the energy of the incoming flow
Prevent floating debris and large objects from entering the waterway
questions.solution:
**To prevent floating debris and large objects from entering the waterway.**

A trash rack is a screen of steel bars set across the intake opening. It intercepts logs, branches, leaves, plastic and any other coarse material carried by the river, which would otherwise:

- **block the penstock** or the turbine's guide vane passages;
- **damage the runner** on impact;
- accumulate and progressively **choke the intake**, starving the plant of water.

Design parameters:

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| **Bar spacing** | Governed by the turbine — roughly **1/20 of the runner blade spacing**; commonly 50–150 mm |
| **Approach velocity** | **0.6 – 1.2 m/s** — slow enough to limit head loss, fast enough that the rack does not silt |
| Inclination | 60° to 80° to the horizontal, so it can be raked |
| Cleaning | Manual rake, or mechanical raking machine on larger plants |

The **bar spacing rule** is the important one: it is set by the machine to be protected, so a high-head **Pelton** with fine nozzles needs a much closer rack than a low-head **Kaplan** with wide blade passages.

**Head loss** across the rack must be included in the energy balance, and it rises sharply as the rack blinds with debris — which is why differential level sensors across the rack trigger cleaning, and why a blocked rack is a real operational hazard rather than a nuisance.

**Where it fits among the intake's defences**, each handling a different size fraction:

| Device | Removes |
|---|---|
| **Trash rack** | **Floating debris, logs, large objects** |
| **Gravel trap** | Coarse **bed load** — gravel and stones |
| **Settling basin** | Finer **suspended sediment**, down to 0.1–0.2 mm |
| Skimmer wall | Surface-floating material |

So the sequence is **coarse to fine**, and the trash rack is the first line. Why the other options are wrong follows directly: dissolved salts are not removed by any intake structure; discharge is measured by a weir or flume; and energy dissipation belongs to structures at a spillway toe.

**Why the whole chain matters so much in Nepal.** Himalayan rivers carry hard **quartz and feldspar** — minerals harder than runner steel — and abrasion damage rises steeply with head. Passing that sediment through a high-head machine destroys the runner profile, cuts efficiency and forces the unit out of service for repair. Hence the settling basin is designed to remove particles down to **0.1 mm for a Pelton** (Set 3 Q50, Q70), and the trash rack and gravel trap upstream of it exist so that the basin is not overwhelmed by material it was never intended to handle.

examTip.trick: A **trash rack** across an intake stops floating debris, branches and ice from entering the waterway and reaching the turbine or the pumps.
examTip.mnemonic: **Bar spacing is set by what must be protected downstream** — coarse for a canal intake, fine for a turbine. It must be **cleaned**, mechanically or by hand: a blocked rack raises the head loss across it sharply, and a partly blocked one creates uneven approach flow and **vortices** at the intake.

questions.stem: The unit speed of a turbine is defined as the speed of the turbine when it works under a head of:
questions.solution:
**1 metre.**

The **unit quantities** are the values a turbine would take if it operated under a head of **unity**. They exist so that performance measured at one head can be transferred to another head on the same machine:

| Unit quantity | Definition | Expression |
|---|---|---|
| **Unit speed** | Speed under **1 m** head | **N_u = N/√H** |
| **Unit discharge** | Discharge under 1 m head | **Q_u = Q/√H** |
| **Unit power** | Power under 1 m head | **P_u = P/H^{3/2}** |

**Where the exponents come from.** Each follows from the physics rather than being arbitrary:

- **Speed:** the runner's peripheral velocity scales with the jet velocity, and v ∝ √(2gH), so **N ∝ √H**.
- **Discharge:** Q = A·v with A fixed for a given machine, so **Q ∝ √H**.
- **Power:** P = ηγQH ∝ √H × H, so **P ∝ H^{3/2}**.

**How they are used.** Since N_u, Q_u and P_u are constants for a *particular* turbine, performance at a new head follows immediately:

> N₁/√H₁ = N₂/√H₂,  Q₁/√H₁ = Q₂/√H₂,  P₁/H₁^{3/2} = P₂/H₂^{3/2}

So a turbine tested at one head — or operating at a reduced reservoir level — can have its speed, discharge and output predicted at any other head without re-testing.

**Do not confuse unit quantities with specific speed.** They answer different questions:

| | **Unit quantities** | **Specific speed** |
|---|---|---|
| Compare | The **same** turbine at **different heads** | **Different** turbines |
| Definition | Values at H = 1 m | **N_s = N√P/H^{5/4}** |
| Use | Predict performance of one machine | **Select the type** of machine |

**Specific speed** is the design-selection parameter, and its bands are the ones examined most often:

| N_s (kW units) | Turbine | Head |
|---|---|---|
| **10 – 35** | **Pelton, single jet** | > 250 m |
| 35 – 60 | Pelton, multi-jet | High |
| 60 – 300 | **Francis** | 25 – 250 m |
| 300 – 1000 | **Kaplan / propeller** | < 25 m |

Set 4 Q65 works a specific-speed calculation (2000 hp at 150 m and 300 rpm giving N_s ≈ 22, hence a Pelton), and Set 3 Q91 the head-based classification that follows from it.

The related idea is **homologous series**: geometrically similar turbines of different size obey the same non-dimensional relations, which is what allows a **model test** in the laboratory to predict the behaviour of a full-size machine — the turbomachinery equivalent of the dynamic similarity discussed in Set 3 Q86.

examTip.trick: The **unit quantities** normalise a turbine's performance to **unit head (1 m)** so that different machines and different operating heads can be compared: **N_u = N/√H**, **Q_u = Q/√H**, **P_u = P/H^(3/2)**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Unit quantities normalise to H = 1 m; SPECIFIC speed N_s = N√P/H^(5/4) identifies the TYPE of machine.** Different purposes: unit quantities compare one turbine at different heads; specific speed tells you whether you are looking at a Pelton, a Francis or a Kaplan.

questions.stem: In traffic volume studies, traffic is commonly expressed in terms of PCU, which stands for:
questions.solution:
**Passenger Car Unit.**

A traffic stream contains vehicles of very different size, speed and manoeuvrability, so a raw vehicle count says little about the demand on the road. The **PCU** converts a mixed stream into an equivalent number of passenger cars, so that volumes and capacities can be compared on one scale.

Equivalency factors (IRC 106), which show how unequal the vehicles are:

| Vehicle | PCU |
|---|---|
| Bicycle | 0.5 |
| Motorcycle / scooter | **0.5** |
| **Passenger car, jeep, van** | **1.0** |
| Auto-rickshaw | 1.2 |
| Light commercial vehicle | 1.4 |
| **Truck or bus** | **3.0** |
| Truck-trailer, agricultural tractor | 4.5 |
| Cycle rickshaw | 2.0 |
| Animal-drawn cart | 6.0 – 8.0 |

**Why a bus counts as three cars.** It is not simply a matter of length. A large vehicle occupies more road space, accelerates and decelerates more slowly, climbs gradients far more slowly, and obstructs overtaking — so it consumes disproportionately more of the road's capacity than its physical size suggests. The factors are correspondingly higher in **hilly terrain**, where the speed differential is greatest.

**Worked illustration.** A count of 200 cars, 50 buses and 100 motorcycles in an hour gives
> 200(1.0) + 50(3.0) + 100(0.5) = 200 + 150 + 50 = **400 PCU/hour**

from a raw count of 350 vehicles — the mix, not the number, being what matters.

**Where PCU is used:**
- Expressing **capacity**: about 2000 PCU/hour per lane for an urban road, 1500 for a rural two-lane road.
- **Design service volume**, from which the number of lanes follows.
- **AADT** (annual average daily traffic) for road classification and prioritisation.
- **Level of service** assessment, and signal design.

Related quantities from the same family of studies: **AADT**, the **30th highest hourly volume** commonly taken as the design hourly volume, and the **peak hour factor** PHF = V/(4V₁₅), whose minimum of 0.25 was derived in Set 1 Q17.

Note the distinct role of the **vehicle damage factor** in *pavement* design, which is a different equivalence entirely: PCU measures a vehicle's demand on **capacity**, whereas the VDF measures its demand on **structural life** through equivalent standard axles. A bus is 3 PCU but may be several standard axles — and it is the axle load, raised to the fourth power, that destroys pavements.

examTip.trick: Different vehicles occupy different amounts of road space and interact differently with traffic, so a raw vehicle count is meaningless. **PCU** converts everything to a common unit.
examTip.mnemonic: **Car 1.0, motorcycle 0.5, bus/truck 3.0, cycle 0.5, cycle rickshaw 1.5, bullock cart 6–8.** In Nepal's mixed traffic the conversion matters enormously — a road carrying mostly motorcycles and one carrying mostly trucks have completely different capacities at the same vehicle count.

questions.stem: The Los Angeles abrasion test on road aggregate measures its resistance to:
questions.solution:
**Wear and attrition.**

The Los Angeles test measures how well an aggregate resists being **worn away** by rubbing and grinding — the action it experiences under traffic at a road surface, where particles are abraded against one another and against tyres.

**Method:** a graded sample together with a specified number of **steel spheres** (the abrasive charge) is placed in a hollow steel drum and rotated for **500 revolutions** at 30 to 33 rpm. The drum has an internal shelf that lifts and drops the charge on each revolution, producing both **impact and grinding**. The percentage of material passing the 1.7 mm sieve afterwards is the **Los Angeles abrasion value** — so a **lower** value means a tougher aggregate.

Permissible limits:

| Layer | Maximum LA value |
|---|---|
| **Bituminous surface course** | **30%** |
| Bituminous base / binder course | 35 – 40% |
| WBM base course | 40 – 50% |
| Concrete pavement wearing surface | 30% |

**The distinction the question is testing** — each aggregate test measures a different mode of attack, and they are routinely confused:

| Test | Measures | Limit (surfacing) |
|---|---|---|
| **Los Angeles abrasion** | **Wear and attrition** | 30% |
| **Aggregate impact value** | Resistance to **sudden shock** | 30% |
| **Aggregate crushing value** | Resistance to **gradual crushing** | 30% |
| **Soundness** | Resistance to **weathering / freeze–thaw** | 12% (Na₂SO₄) |
| Water absorption | Porosity | 2% |
| Flakiness / elongation index | Particle **shape** | 25% / 15% |
| **Polished stone value** | Resistance to **polishing** — skid resistance | Minimum 55 |

So impact and crushing tests measure **strength**, soundness measures **durability under weather** (Set 3 Q23), and only the Los Angeles test addresses **wear** — which is precisely why it governs the wearing course.

**Why wear resistance matters most at the surface.** The wearing course is in direct contact with tyres, so abrasion there determines how long the surface texture — and hence the **skid resistance** — survives. An aggregate that abrades quickly polishes smooth, and a polished surface loses friction in the wet, which is a safety failure rather than merely a maintenance one. That is why the **polished stone value** is specified alongside the abrasion value for surfacing aggregate, and why hard, angular, non-polishing rock is sought for the top layer even where softer material is acceptable lower down.

examTip.trick: The LA machine tumbles aggregate with steel balls, so it combines **impact, grinding and rubbing** — that is, resistance to **wear and attrition** over time under traffic.
examTip.mnemonic: **LA abrasion = WEAR. Impact value = SHOCK. Crushing value = gradual LOAD. Soundness = WEATHERING (freeze–thaw and salt).** Four tests for four different durability demands. LA limits: **30% for wearing courses, 50% for base courses.**

questions.stem: The sand replacement method is used in road construction to determine the:
options: Optimum moisture content of the subgrade
In-situ (field) dry density of a compacted layer
questions.solution:
**The in-situ (field) dry density of a compacted layer.**

The sand replacement method answers the question every earthworks specification turns on: **has this layer actually been compacted to the required density?**

**Method (IS 2720 Part 28):** a small hole is excavated in the compacted layer and the extracted soil is weighed and its moisture content determined. The hole's **volume** is then measured by filling it with **uniform, free-running standard sand** of known bulk density from a calibrated pouring cylinder. Then

> Bulk density = mass of excavated soil / volume of hole
> **Dry density = bulk density / (1 + w)**

**How the result is used.** The field dry density is compared with the laboratory maximum dry density from the **Proctor test** to give the **degree of compaction**:

> **Relative compaction = γ_d(field) / γ_d(max) × 100%**

against the specified requirement — typically **95% of MDD** for an embankment or subgrade and **98%** for a base course (Set 3 Q14, Q9).

So the two tests work as a pair: **Proctor in the laboratory sets the target; sand replacement in the field checks it.**

The field density methods compared:

| Method | Suits | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **Sand replacement** | **Any soil**, including gravelly | The general-purpose reference method |
| **Core cutter** | **Cohesive** soils only | Quick, but a cutter cannot be driven into gravel |
| Water displacement / rubber balloon | Any soil | Volume measured by water |
| **Nuclear density gauge** | Any soil | Fast, non-destructive; needs calibration and radiation licensing |

Why the other options name different tests: **OMC** comes from the **Proctor** test; **bearing capacity / subgrade strength** from the **CBR** test (Set 3 Q97) or a plate load test; **gradation** from **sieve analysis**.

**Why this matters more than it appears.** Inadequate compaction is the single most common cause of pavement **rutting** (Set 3 Q5) and of embankment settlement — the layer densifies further under traffic, and those small permanent strains accumulate into a visible failure. Because compaction is invisible once the next layer is placed, **field density testing is the only means of verifying it**, which is why specifications prescribe a testing frequency (commonly one test per 500 to 1000 m² per layer) and why the records form part of the contractual quality-assurance file.

Note too that the test must be accompanied by a **moisture content** determination taken at the same time: density alone means little unless the layer was compacted near its **optimum moisture content**, since that is the condition under which the target MDD is attainable at all.

examTip.trick: The sand replacement method measures **field dry density** by excavating a small hole, weighing the soil removed, and finding the hole's volume from the weight of calibrated sand that fills it.
examTip.mnemonic: **Sand replacement for GRAVELLY or HARD soil; CORE CUTTER for soft fine soil** (the cutter has to be driven in, which fails in stone). The result is compared with the laboratory maximum as **relative compaction γ_d/γ_dmax**, with **95–100%** typically specified.

questions.stem: An engineer who has a financial interest in a firm bidding for a project he is evaluating should:
options: Proceed, provided the evaluation is technically sound
Accept the assignment but reduce his fee
Keep the interest confidential to avoid embarrassment
Disclose the interest and withdraw from the evaluation
questions.solution:
**Disclose the interest and withdraw from the evaluation.**

This is a **conflict of interest**, and the required response has two parts, both necessary:

1. **Disclose** — promptly, fully and in writing, to the client or employer.
2. **Withdraw** from the decision, so that judgement is exercised by someone with no personal stake in the outcome.

Disclosure without withdrawal is insufficient here, because the engineer would still be deciding a matter in which he stands to gain. Withdrawal without disclosure is also insufficient, since the client cannot then assess whether earlier work was affected.

**Why technical soundness is not the test.** Option (a) is the tempting answer and the wrong one. The objection to a conflict of interest is not that the engineer *will* decide dishonestly — he may well be scrupulous — but that **neither he nor anyone else can demonstrate that he did not**. Public confidence in the process depends on the appearance of impartiality as much as its reality, and once the interest is known the evaluation is worthless whatever its content. Option (c) compounds the fault by concealment, and (b) misunderstands the problem entirely: the issue is the **decision**, not the fee.

**The governing principles**, from the NEC code of ethics and the professional codes generally:

| Principle | Content |
|---|---|
| **Public safety paramount** | Hold the safety, health and welfare of the public above all |
| **Faithful agent** | Act faithfully for each client, and **disclose all conflicts of interest** |
| Integrity | Avoid deceptive acts; accept **no bribes, gifts or secret commissions** |
| Competence | Practise only within your area of competence |
| Objectivity | Public statements truthful and objective |

**Other situations of the same kind**, worth recognising: accepting payment from **more than one party** for the same service without the knowledge of both; accepting **gifts or hospitality** from a contractor whose work you supervise or certify; **reviewing your own** design in the capacity of an independent checker; and taking on private work that competes with your employer's.

**Consequences in Nepal.** The **Nepal Engineering Council Act 2055** makes professional misconduct a disciplinary matter, and the Council may **suspend or cancel registration** — which removes the right to practise. Public procurement adds a further layer: the **Public Procurement Act 2063** requires evaluation committee members to declare conflicts and stand down, and a tender evaluated by a conflicted official is liable to be **annulled**.

The general test to carry into practice: *if the interest would embarrass you were it discovered later, it must be disclosed now.*

examTip.trick: A conflict of interest is not resolved by trying to be impartial — it is resolved by **disclosure and removal from the decision**. Remaining involved after disclosing is still a conflict.
examTip.mnemonic: **Disclose AND withdraw — both, not either.** This follows from the first principle of every engineering code: **the safety, health and welfare of the PUBLIC is paramount**, above duty to client, employer or self. An engineer who cannot be seen to be impartial cannot serve that duty, however honest their intentions.
